articles.title: Russia employs thousands of North Koreans to build combat drones, sanctions monitors say
articles.body:
Russia is increasingly using North Korean citizens to assemble combat drones for its war against Ukraine, circumventing international sanctions while providing Pyongyang with an important source of foreign currency, according to a report published by the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT) on Sept. 16. Over the past year, North Korean migrant workers abroad generated as much as $800 million for Kim Jong Un’s government, which used the funds to finance nuclear and missile programs in violation of UN Security Council resolutions, the report states.
The report estimates that as many as 25,000 North Koreans are employed in Russia’s drone industry, including at facilities in the Alabuga special economic zone in Tatarstan, where Geran-type attack drones, modeled on Iran’s Shahed series, are assembled. Russia gains a new pool of workers for industries supporting its war against Ukraine while further eroding a sanctions regime against Pyongyang that Moscow itself once helped enforce.
According to the MSMT, North Korean workers in Russia are often categorized as students under a special visa arrangement that allows sanctions to be circumvented without the need for a formal breach. One “student” worker earns an average of about $7,500 a year, the report said, with most of that money confiscated by the North Korean government.
Monthly pay in Russia can be up to five times higher than in China, making Russia an increasingly attractive destination for Pyongyang to send such laborers. Still, as of the end of 2025, between 20,000 and 70,000 North Koreans were working in China, compared with 15,000 to 30,000 in Russia.
“DPRKauthorities also exercise extreme control over labourers’ movement and interactions with outsiders in order to prevent defections, while labourers who do defect risk reprisals against family members remaining in North Korea,” the report said.
It was previously reported that North Korean workers at construction sites in three Russian cities were working up to 16 hours a day with virtually no days off and receiving no more than $10 a month after deductions. Their passports were confiscated by representatives of North Korean security services, and the workers often did not know who their actual employer was because Russian companies hired them in violation of UN sanctions.
The MSMT, which includes the United States, South Korea, Japan and eight other countries, was established in 2024 after Russia blocked the renewal of the mandate for a UN panel that had monitored compliance with sanctions against Pyongyang for 15 years.

articles.title: Poland scrambles military aircraft due to Russian attack on western Ukraine
articles.body:
The Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces reported that due to Russian strikes on the western regions of Ukraine, military aviation operations have commenced in Polish airspace, and ground-based air defense and radar reconnaissance systems have been placed on alert.
"Due to the strikes carried out by Russia using jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles against the western territory of Ukraine, military aviation operations have begun in Polish airspace," the Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces stated in a post on the social network X on Thursday.
The command noted that the necessary forces and assets available to the air forces have been activated, while ground-based air defense systems and radar reconnaissance systems have also been placed on a state of readiness.
It was emphasized that these actions are preventive in nature and aimed at ensuring the security of airspace and protecting it. The Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces stated that it is monitoring the current situation and that subordinate forces and assets remain ready for immediate response.
On the night of Thursday, September 17, Russian occupiers attacked Ukraine with Onyx missiles, ballistic missiles, Kalibrs, 157 drones, and a dozen "Banderoly" drones, targeting the Kyiv region, Zaporizhia, and the Odesa region.
Recent massive Russian attacks on the western regions of Ukraine took place during the day on September 12 and on the night of September 13, 2026, lasting for over 24 hours. The enemy deployed hundreds of drones, including Shahed-type strike drones and jet-powered UAVs, targeting Volyn, Lviv (including Stry), Ivano-Frankivsk, Ternopil, Khmelnytsky, Rivne, and Zhytomyr regions.

articles.title: Trump claims US nears 'end' of Iran war, holding 'direct talks'
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump claimed to media that the US is “hopefully toward the end” of its war with Iran and notes that he has spoken with them "directly". Meanwhile, Iran's national security chief Mohsen Rezaei says the US must take practical steps to earn Tehran’s confidence, stressing that the country harbours zero trust in Washington.
Israeli military chief Eyal Zamir says Israeli forces will continue operating deep inside Lebanon despite any ceasefire agreements
The war in Yemen continues as Houthi advances are unaffected by the Saudi-led coalition airstrikes
Israeli attacks continue on Gaza, occupied West Bank, and southern Syria
And so we continue our live coverage...
Syria offers cheaper diesel after fuel-price protests
Syria will offer cheaper diesel for heating, agriculture and industry, Energy Minister Mohammed al-Bashir said on Thursday, days after a fuel price hike triggered the most widespread protests since the fall of Bashar al-Assad.
The move signals a partial retreat by the government after last weekend's increases sparked demonstrations across the country, with protesters burning tyres, blocking roads and demanding the rises be reversed. About 90% of Syrians live below the poverty line, according to UN estimates.
Bashir told a press conference that diesel would be sold at three prices — 115, 150 and 175 Syrian pounds per litre — depending on its specifications and intended use, after a meeting with President Ahmed al-Sharaa on the fuel crisis on Wednesday night.
The government had raised the standard diesel price by 40% on Saturday to 175 pounds per litre from 125, alongside increases of about 26% to 28% for gasoline and about 9% for household and industrial gas.
Bashir said diesel produced by local refineries would be sold at 115 Syrian pounds per litre for heating, agriculture and other eligible users. A second grade, secured with the help of what he described as "friendly countries", would be sold at 150 pounds per litre for productive and service sectors and heavy machinery.
The standard grade would remain at 175 pounds per litre, while gasoline and gas prices would remain unchanged.
Syrian Energy Minister Mohammed al-Bashir [Getty]
Bank of England warns of hike if Iran war persists
The Bank of England held its benchmark interest rate at 3.75 percent on Thursday, but warned that a hike might be needed as the Middle East war pushes up energy prices.
The widely expected decision following a regular monetary policy meeting comes after the Federal Reserve on Wednesday lifted US interest rates for the first time since 2023, citing the need to combat surging inflation.
"So far higher energy costs have had a limited effect on price and wage setting in the UK," Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey said.
"But the longer this volatility persists, the bigger the impact it will have on inflation, and the more likely it is we will need to raise" the benchmark rate, he added.
Surging energy prices triggered by the Middle East war have led central banks around the world to shift in favour of tightening monetary policy.
Yemen's Houthis say government strikes kill 3 children
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis said Thursday three children had been killed in government strikes, according to the group's media.
"Three children were killed and several Yemeni nationals were injured in strikes by the Saudi-backed mercenaries," in the Taiz province, according to Almasirah television. Earlier, the broadcaster said Saudi airstrikes had killed one person.
Israeli minister suggests Turkey take in Hamas members
Israel's defence minister suggested on Thursday that Turkey take in Hamas members from Gaza, as he called for the full-scale removal of the war-torn territory's two million people—a war crime.
The comments by Israel Katz, who is known for his xenophobic remarks, came after an increase in tensions between Turkey and Israel.
"Israel will continue to act to complete its security objectives and ensure that the threat of October 7 cannot return," Katz wrote on X.
Katz added that if Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan "wants to help his brothers in creed and path in Gaza—let him invite them to move to Antalya. A lot of space has opened up there in the absence of Israeli tourists".
Antalya, a beach town at the heart of Turkey's tourism industry, was a top destination for Israelis before relations deteriorated over Israel's genocide of Gaza.
Israel continues to attack the Gaza Strip. [Getty]
Quadcopters: Israel's weapon for indiscriminate killing
Since 7 October 2023, the Israeli military has increased its use of drones known as "quadcopters" in the Gaza Strip, after previously deploying them in eastern and border areas.
This type of drone has been used extensively and on an unprecedented scale, are of multiple types, and their use has are not limited to attacking resistance fighters.
One person, a Yemeni resident, was killed and two others injured in a drone interception in Saudi Arabia’s southwestern governorate of Taif, Saudi state TV says.
It is the first death announced in Saudi Arabia this month since the Iran-backed Houthis in neighbouring Yemen launched attacks.
Pakistan defence minister: time to implement Mecca pact
Pakistan's Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said it's time to implement the Mecca agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkye due to recent Houthi attacks.
Speaking with Pakistani TV channel Geo News, Asif said Islamabad remains committed to protecting Saudi Arabia and its holy sites, adding that even without an agreement, it was a duty to protect them.
China pressing Iran to rein in Houthis after Saudi appeal
China has privately asked Tehran to help rein in Yemen's Houthis after an appeal to Beijing by Saudi Arabia following the Iran-backed group’s military blitz in the past week, according to three Iranian sources familiar with the matter.
Riyadh turned to China for help after the Houthis made rapid advances along the Red Sea coast and around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, moves that have left Saudi oil exports and shipping more exposed, the sources say.
China has publicly called for restraint, dialogue and the restoration of safe navigation, but its private message went further than the public statements, they say.
The sources, who have been briefed on the discussions and have spoken on condition of anonymity, do not provide details of how the message was delivered or whether it was conveyed during a visit to China yesterday by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.
The sources say Tehran's response was that stability and peace in the region depend on ending the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Ireland broadcaster will boycott 2027 Eurovision over Israel
Ireland will boycott the Eurovision Song Contest for a second year over Israel's participation, the country's national broadcaster says.
RTE said Thursday it will not send an act to the 2027 competition in Bulgaria and will not broadcast the show because of the "appalling and ongoing loss of lives in Gaza."
Israel and Morocco said they will open embassies and expand relations established under the U.S.-brokered Abraham Accords, which saw four Arab countries normalize ties with Israel in 2020.
Israel and Morocco announced the move in a joint statement with the United States, saying that integrating Israel into the broader Arab world “will lead to peace, stability and shared prosperity.” The Abraham Accords were a marquee foreign policy achievement of President Donald Trump’s first term.
Israel and Morocco face elections in the coming weeks.
The Ministry of Health in Gaza said five Palestinians were killed and 28 wounded in the past 24 hours by Israeli attacks, including three new deaths and two people who succumbed to their wounds.
Since a ceasefire took effect on October 2025, the ministry said at least 1,386 Palestinians have been killed and 4,784 wounded by Israel, with 831 bodies retrieved from under the rubble.
The ministry added that the collapse of the Saada building had left 21 dead, and injured more than 14 others, with several people still missing, bringing the total death toll from building collapses to 61.
Iran gave a Swedish diplomat in Tehran 48 hours to leave the country on Thursday after Sweden expelled a staff member from the Iranian embassy in Stockholm.
The Swedish ambassador was summoned to the foreign ministry in Tehran to protest against the Swedish decision, which is "unjustified and contrary to international law", Iran's foreign ministry said in a statement broadcast by state television.
Israel adds tender for 2,167 housing units to settlements
Israel has added a tender for 2,167 housing units to its E1 settlement expansion plan, Israeli rights groups said of a project that "buries" any potential Palestinian state.
The project would bisect the Israeli-occupied West Bank and cut it off from East Jerusalem, fragmenting the land Palestinians hope will form the heart of a state.
The tender for 2,167 units is in addition to a tender for 1,234 units announced at the end of August, bringing the total number of housing units to 3,401, Israeli rights group Ir Amim said in a statement issued late on Wednesday.
The decision was condemned by a representative for Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas on Thursday who said the E1 tenders were in violation of international law.
Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, an ultra-nationalist in the governing right-wing coalition, has said the plan would "bury" a Palestinian state.
The tender is scheduled to open for bidding on 25 October, two days before Israel is due to hold a parliamentary election.
PA condemns 'unjustified' US visa denial for Abbas
The Palestinian Authority slams a decision by the United States to refuse to grant visas for its officials to attend the UN General Assembly in New York next week, a move that includes President Mahmoud Abbas.
In a statement, the Palestinian Authority foreign ministry calls it "an unjustified measure that runs counter to efforts to rebuild trust, develop Palestinian-US relations, and create the necessary political climate for implementing the two-state solution and achieving peace and stability."
Turkey's Defence Ministry condemned a Houthi drone attack targeting Saudi Arabia and other actions by the group, calling for an end to such acts that threaten regional stability.
The ministry said the continued Houthi threat in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab was negatively affecting not only regional security but also international maritime trade and global stability.
Houthis have gained ground in Yemen over the past few days. [Getty]
Israeli election is a contest over how to continue genocide
Despite Gadi Eisenkot emerging as Netanyahu’s strongest challenger in the Israeli elections, his political agenda won't change the current genocidal course, writes Yara Hawari.
Budget carrier Wizz Air on Thursday said it had cut its planned capacity for the second half of its fiscal year by 5%, joining rivals in scaling back growth plans as the Iran war continues to drive a sharp rise in fuel costs.
The worst airline crisis in terms of costs since the COVID-19 pandemic, the U.S.-Iran war has sent the global aviation industry into a severe cost shock, with Latvian airline airBaltic becoming the first European carrier to file for bankruptcy earlier this week due to the conflict.
While full-service flag carriers have generally proved more resilient than budget operators, whose business models rely on cheap fares, even larger U.S. carriers have scaled back their planned flight schedules as surging fuel prices threaten earnings.
Wizz Air upgraded its revenue per available seat kilometre (RASK) forecast for the second quarter running from July to September to flat year-on-year, from a previous forecast of "down low single digits," after a stronger-than-expected summer revenue performance, sending shares up more than 3% in early trade.
The Hungarian airline set out medium-term financial targets of achieving €10 billion ($11.47 billion) in revenue and a 10% EBIT margin by fiscal year 2030 as it seeks to restore sustainable profitability after a turbulent stretch.
It also plans to operate an all-new-engine-option fleet of 335 aircraft and carry 127 million passengers by fiscal year 2030, up from the 269 aircraft it currently operates and the 69.7 million passengers it carried in its last financial year.
UN mission believes US committed war crimes in Iran
A UN fact-finding mission on Iran said on Thursday it had reasonable grounds to believe the United States was behind two military strikes on a school and sports facility in Iran in February, and that these constituted war crimes.
It also found that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests.
The findings in a new report by the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran, to be submitted to the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, examined the US's conduct during the Iran war that began in February and the Iranian government's response to nationwide unrest that begun in late December.
The UN experts said they found reasonable grounds to believe US forces were responsible for an attack on the Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in the city of Minab, where more than 150 people were killed, including around 120 schoolchildren, according to Iranian officials.
The attack constituted an indiscriminate attack causing civilian deaths and damage to civilian infrastructure, amounting to a war crime under international law, the mission concluded.
According to the report, the US relied on intelligence suggesting a senior Iranian military commander was present at the site but failed to adequately verify the information before launching the strike. Investigators said the failure to update targeting intelligence and confirm the building was a military objective amounted to more than mere negligence.
"Rather, the US directed the strikes at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen."
Turkey to suspend all flights by Iran's largest carrier
Turkish authorities have directed Mahan Air, Iran's largest carrier, to suspend all flights to Turkey, a person familiar with the matter told the Associated Press Thursday, marking one of the most consequential disruptions yet to Tehran's already battered aviation industry.
Key US House Democrat refuses to clear $2.8 billion sale
US Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the US House of Representatives Foreign Affairs Committee, is obstructing a Trump administration proposal for a $2.8 billion bomb sale to Israel.
Meeks says he will not clear the transaction due to concerns that these 2,000-pound munitions will not be used in accordance with US and international law.
The proposal, he adds, raised questions "about how these munitions could be used in densely populated areas of Gaza and Lebanon."
Iran's Araqchi, Pakistan army chief discuss developments
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi and Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir discussed the latest regional developments in a phone call during Araqchi's visit to Beijing on Wednesday, Iranian media reported, as US-Iran negotiations remain stalled with no agreement in sight.
Houthis say Saudi strikes killed one, targeted telecom tower
Saudi strikes in Yemen killed one person and targeted three telecommunications towers on Thursday, according to Houthi media.
"Saudi enemy warplanes targeted three telecommunications towers" in Taiz province, while one civilian was killed and another injured in strikes on the town of Abs, Almasirah television said.
Lebanon, France, Jordan to discuss struggling Lebanese army
The heads of state of Lebanon, France and Jordan will meet Thursday in Paris as part of an effort to drum up support for the struggling Lebanese military.
A donor conference for Lebanon's cash-strapped army was initially set to take place in February, led by France, Saudi Arabia and the United States. However, it was postponed following the eruption of the Iran war.
The Lebanese army has now found itself caught between the Israeli military—occupying much of southern Lebanon—and Hezbollah, which refused calls to give up its weapons until Israel makes a full withdrawal.
Thursday's meeting in Paris will center on preparing the ground for a donor conference. It will also focus on the situation in southern Lebanon and plans for an international presence there after the mandate of the UN peacekeeping force known as UNIFIL expires at the end of the year, Lebanese President Joseph Aoun's office said in a statement.
Yemeni forces clash with Houthis near Saudi border
Yemeni government forces clashed with Houthi fighters near the Saudi border, with AFP footage showing soldiers in armoured vehicles and trucks pushing across desert terrain under the crackle of machine-gun fire.
The Houthis also released footage on Wednesday of the fighting in the northwestern Al-Jawf area, as well as a video purporting to show the downing of a fighter jet belonging to Saudi Arabia, the group's longtime foe and the Yemeni government's main backer.
The group has recently made major gains in a lightning offensive that Saudi airstrikes have failed to roll back, leaving the Yemeni government scrambling to respond.
"The First Division Emergency Forces are advancing on the Al-Labanat front and, God willing, will reach Houthi positions," Waleed Al-Mahajeri, operations commander of the government's Fifth Brigade, told an embedded AFP journalist on Tuesday.
AFP footage showed the soldiers firing heavy machine guns, artillery and RPGs at distant targets, as well as the bodies of Houthi fighters and entrenchments the government forces said the group had abandoned as they fell back.
"Al-Masariya Hill has been liberated, as has Al-Labanat camp, and the advance is continuing," said soldier Abu Mithaq.
Two sources from the government's military later told AFP on condition of anonymity that government forces were in control of the lower points of Al-Labanat camp, located on a hill, but were facing difficulty seizing control of the rest, as the Houthis held the higher ground.
Taking the camp would be a strategic win for the government forces, as it would clear the path to Al-Hazm, the capital of Al-Jawf governorate, just 50 kilometres (30 miles) away.
Trump to hold talks on Iran with Gulf leaders next week
US President Donald Trump is expected to meet Gulf leaders on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday to discuss the next steps in the Iran war, Axios reported late on Wednesday, citing sources.
The meeting is expected to focus on US ideas for a postwar strategy, Axios reported.

articles.title: Fresh Russian Strikes Hit Ukraine As US House Passes Sanctions Bill Targeting Moscow
articles.body:
Russia resumed its missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian cities on September 17, hours after the US Congress passed a sanctions package that supporters say will increase pressure on Moscow and countries that help it finance its war against Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said it was "symbolic" that the US House of Representatives passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 amid another Russian ballistic missile and drone attack on Ukraine.
He said Russian strikes hit civilian and energy infrastructure in eight regions, damaging homes in the capital, Kyiv, and the major southern port city of Odesa and injuring dozens of people, including children.
"The Lindsey Graham bill, along with other strong sanctions steps by our partners against the source of this war -- against Russia -- is an extremely powerful tool that can stop this terrorist war and bring Russia to the point where it has to make peace," Zelenskyy wrote in a post on X.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha welcomed the passage of the Russia sanctions bill, calling it a strong response to Moscow's continued attacks on Ukraine.
However, he also urged further sanctions, including a full embargo, restrictions on Russia's so-called shadow fleet, and blocking sanctions targeting its military-industrial complex.
"We can stop Putin by depriving him of the resources to continue this war," Sybiha wrote on X.
Following the latest Russian attack, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said 18 people, including children, had been injured in the city, while a repeat drone strike sparked a fire in an administrative building.
In Odesa, regional authorities said a Russian overnight strike injured six people, including two children, and damaged residential buildings, a private home, and infrastructure.
Zaporizhzhya, in southeastern Ukraine, was also hit by a Russian missile strike that injured three people and damaged industrial facilities, according to regional authorities.
Later in the day, regional Governor Mykhaylo Semikin said at least five more people were injured when a Russian first-person-view (FPV) drone hit a bus carrying civilians.
Meanwhile, Russian officials reported that a Ukrainian drone attack damaged an oil refinery in the Russian city of Yaroslavl.
Authorities in Russia's Krasnodar region said drone debris sparked a fire at an oil refinery, which was quickly extinguished. No injuries reported.
The refinery, located about 250 kilometers northeast of Moscow, had previously been targeted by Ukrainian drones and halted processing at two of its three crude distillation units following the August attack.
Zelenskyy confirmed the attack on the Yaroslavl oil refinery, adding that Ukraine's Security Service had carried out a strike on a military airfield in Rostov, in southern Russia near the Ukrainian border, damaging three planes and three helicopters.
The attacks that targeted energy facilities in Russia and Ukraine followed US President Donald Trump's announcement of an energy truce between the two countries on September 14, although neither side has confirmed such an agreement.
Trump had earlier urged Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian diesel infrastructure, saying the attacks had caused a diesel shortage that was “hurting the world.”
Since the beginning of the summer, Ukrainian drone strikes have caused nationwide fuel shortages in Russia and stoked discontent among citizens who had previously been largely insulated from the war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year.

articles.title: Russia using North Korean laborers on student visas to illicitly build drones, report says
articles.body:
Russia using North Korean laborers on student visas to illicitly build drones, report says
Russia is increasingly using North Korean laborers to manufacture military drones in violation of international sanctions against North Korea, according to a report published by the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team on Sept. 16.
The Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team is a group of 11 countries, including the United States, that monitors and reports on efforts to evade U.N. sanctions against North Korea and its allies.
According to the report, Russia "created a student visa scheme to camouflage North Korean laborers in Russia as students." The scheme generates revenue for North Korea that can be used to fund Pyongyang's "unlawful weapons programs," the report says.
Russia and North Korea have established an "extensive ecosystem of state-led sanctions evasion activities and corruption," the report says. This includes "utilizing student and tourist visas instead of work permits, adjusting Russian law to allow those on student visas to earn income," and "bribing Russian universities."
An estimated 15,000 to 30,000 North Korean workers were employed illegally in Russia in 2025, according to the report. The majority were "manufacturing military drones for Russia on Russian soil," including at the Alabuga drone plant in Tatarstan.
The report estimates that Pyongyang's illicit overseas labor program generated between $450 million and $800 million in 2025 alone. Each North Korean worker employed illegally in Russia generated an estimated $7,500 in annual wages, according to the report.
North Korea has become one of Moscow's closest allies since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. It is the only country to have officially sent troops to support Russia's war, while also supplying large quantities of military equipment, including ballistic missiles, artillery shells and rocket launchers.
In April, North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un opened a museum honoring North Korean soldiers who fought alongside Russian forces in the war against Ukraine.

articles.title: Up to 25,000 North Koreans may be making military drones in Russia. Sanctions monitors say they enter on student visas.
articles.body:
Up to 25,000 North Koreans may be making military drones in Russia. Sanctions monitors say they enter on student visas.
As many as 25,000 North Korean citizens may be working in military drone production in Russia, including at the Alabuga special economic zone in Tatarstan, according to a report by the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT), which includes the United States, South Korea, Japan, and eight other countries.
The report says North Korean workers enter Russia on student visas under a scheme that allows them to circumvent U.N. sanctions. They can earn up to five times more in Russia than in neighboring China. Each worker earns an average of about $7,500 a year, most of which the North Korean authorities take.
As of late 2025, between 15,000 and 30,000 North Korean citizens were working in Russia, while between 20,000 and 70,000 were working in China. The report says North Koreans working abroad earned up to $800 million in 2025 and that North Korea uses the money to fund its nuclear and ballistic missile programs.

articles.title: Russia Employs 25,000 North Koreans in Drone Production
articles.body:
The South Korean SBS News site has reported that as many as 100,000 North Koreans are working in China and Russia, with the latter employing up to 25,000 of them assembling Iranian-designed drones at the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Russia’s Tatarstan as well as Russian arms manufacturing, steel processing facilities, and shipbuilding plants.
The claim is based on a report published by the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT) on Wednesday, Sept. 16 (MSMT), excerpts of which are also cited by Bloomberg.

The Russian Foreign Ministry is said to have issued over 36,400 visas to North Koreans in 2025 – nearly four times the number issued the previous year. According to the report, 98% of visas issued by Russia to North Korea were for “students,” in an attempt to circumvent international sanctions.
The movements of these workers and any interaction with outsiders is strictly controlled. Those who break the rules or attempt to flee risk reprisals being inflicted on their relatives remaining in North Korea (DPRK).
The average salary offered by Russia is around $7,500 per year, which is assessed as around five times that paid in China, most, if not all, is confiscated by Kim Jong Un’s regime, leaving the workers in debt to the state.
The provision of this labor support is yet another example of the cooperation between Moscow and Pyongyang that included arms supply and troop deployments in return for financial and technical support for North Korea’s ballistic missile programs – which some estimates put as high as $800 million last year. While much of this makes its way back to the DPRK through its opaque banking system, the MSMT details instances of cash being physically transported in diplomatic vehicles and pouches, as well as by overseas business travelers.

articles.title: Britain is pushing for air defense coalition to deploy NATO contingent in Ukraine — expert
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 17. /TASS/. Against the backdrop of statements by former Defense Secretary Ben Wallace on the need to shoot down Russian drones over Ukraine, the United Kingdom is calling for the creation of a new air defense coalition, which could serve as a pretext for deploying a NATO contingent in Kiev-controlled territory, Alexander Stepanov, a military expert at the Institute of Law and National Security at the Russian Presidential Academy of National Economy and Public Administration (RANEPA), told TASS.
"It now appears that a certain air defense coalition will be formed under the auspices of the United Kingdom. Such a move is aimed at establishing a military presence and creating conditions for the deployment of a NATO contingent in territory controlled by the Kiev regime," the expert said.
According to him, similar coalitions have been formed in the past – the "coalition of the willing" as a key platform and the F-16 coalition. The current initiative follows the same logic, creating conditions to test the possibility of stationing a contingent under a pretext of allegedly protecting the airspace. Stepanov noted that this highlights the dire state of the Ukrainian armed forces and their inability to independently defend their airspace amid the dominance of Russian precision-guided systems, including Geran drones and long-range ballistic missiles.
"The United Kingdom assumes that these units will not be targeted for elimination and will not be considered legitimate targets by the Russian side. This is a major mistake. Any such action, any such military activity, will be suppressed, and there are enough Geran drones to target all systems--including British ones--that attempt to seal off the airspace over the territory still controlled by the Kiev regime," the expert concluded.
Earlier, former British Secretary of Defense Ben Wallace stated in an interview with the Daily Mail that Britain should shoot down Russian drones over Ukraine. "There is nothing to stop a country shooting down incoming missiles or drones over Ukraine," he said.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: "I don't see China pushing Russia to stop the war"
articles.body:
Zelenskyy: "I don't see China pushing Russia to stop the war"
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy believes that China could push Russia towards peace but is not doing so, and that Beijing is, politically, more on Russia's side.
Source: Zelenskyy on X (Twitter)
Quote: "I saw a real missile made by North Korea in Ukraine. I did not see a Chinese missile. But I know that their technologies get to Russia. The machinery they use comes from China, likely along with smart people and technologies.
I don't see China pushing Russia to stop the war. I never saw that. Maybe they do that during some of their bilateral meetings. I don't know. But I think that they have huge influence over Russia, especially now, when there are a lot of sanctions, the shadow fleet, and cut-off energy and banking systems. Of course, China can find a way to push Putin towards negotiations. I'm sure, but they didn't do it. And if you can and don't, is it support or not?"
Details: Zelenskyy said China is not politically on Ukraine's side in this war: "And it's a pity because this war can be stopped immediately by strong leaders, including China. It's a pity that they are not on our side."
Meanwhile, he believes that the main problem is that China is "not in the middle", but somewhat more on Russia's side: "I mean, not to give weapons directly, but to be more open to them, more helpful to them than to us – for such a big country, a little bit is a lot."
Background: In early July, Zelenskyy said he had spoken with the US president and European leaders at a NATO summit about China's possible role and capabilities in the negotiations to end Russian aggression against Ukraine.

articles.title: Up to 25,000 North Koreans work in Russian drone production
articles.body:
Up to 25,000 North Koreans work in Russian drone production
Russia is recruiting North Korean workers to manufacture drones used in the war against Ukraine by bringing them into the country on student visas. Up to 25,000 North Korean workers are currently employed in drone production at the Alabuga Special Economic Zone (SEZ) in Russia's Tatarstan.
Source: a report by the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT); a joint statement on the report
Quote: "North Korean overseas labourers are reportedly employed in Russia's manufacturing industry including as many as 25,000 North Korean labourers at a widely-sanctioned Russian drone factory in Alabuga, Tatarstan…
The DPRK has promoted the deployment of labourers to Russian Geran-2 drone factories in the Alabuga SEZ in Tatarstan, Russia since 2025."
Details: According to the MSMT report on North Korea's overseas labour programme, Russia currently hosts between 15,000 and 30,000 North Korean workers, linked to 70-80 DPRK companies.
Most are employed in construction, agriculture and similar sectors. However, up to 1,000 workers are employed at strategically important businesses, including weapons manufacturing plants, steel processing facilities or shipbuilding complexes.
Russia currently ranks second worldwide in terms of the number of North Korean overseas workers, behind only China. The number of North Korean workers in Russia has risen particularly sharply since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Russia sends some of them to work in roles supporting its military-industrial complex.
North Koreans work within the Alabuga special economic zone, which is involved in supplying Russian forces with drones used in the war against Ukraine. In 2025, for instance, Russia completed construction of a large residential complex at Alabuga to house foreign workers, including North Korean citizens.
On average, a North Korean worker earns around US$7,500 a year in Russia, although almost all of this income is seized for the benefit of the North Korean regime.
Over recent years, Russia and North Korea have built up an extensive system combining state-level sanctions evasion with corrupt practices. For example, instead of work permits, Russia uses student and tourist visas to bring in North Koreans. In 2025, almost all North Korean workers entered Russia on student visas, posing as international students.
According to the report, intermediaries from third countries may also be involved in recruiting and dispatching North Korean workers to Russia. At least one such case is known to have occurred in Belarus.
Background: The BBC reported earlier that North Korean workers who have fled the country told the BBC about slave-like working conditions in Russia, where they are sent to fill the labour shortage exacerbated by Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukraine Suffers More Civilian Deaths in 8 Months of 2026 Than All of 2025 – UN
articles.body:
August has been one of the deadliest months for civilian casualties in Ukraine, with at least 372 civilians killed and 2,349 injured, a new UN Human Rights for the High Commissioner (HRMMU) report says.
The report, published on Thursday, Sept. 17, says the figure marks a slight decrease from July, which saw the highest toll on ordinary civilians since Russia’s war in Ukraine began, topping the previous high in June.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
This year’s figure – more than the entirety of 2025 within just eight months – is 55 percent higher than during the same period last year and more than double the figure for the same period in 2024, it adds.
More drones, more deaths?
The report says most casualties came from “long-range weapons,” with most documented in cities rather than the frontline areas.
“In August, long-range weapons (missiles and drones) remained the leading cause of civilian casualties, accounting for 47 percent of the total (194 killed; 1,077 injured),” it says. “Most casualties from these weapons occurred far from the frontline in urban centers.”
The spike coincides with Russia’s increased use of drones – latterly the jet-powered variants – and ballistic missiles.
In May, Russia hit Ukraine with record waves of drones, launching over 1,400 in 24 hours. While subsequent waves have seen smaller total numbers, the rise of jet-powered and ballistic drones, coupled with non-stop strikes, has made interception increasingly difficult.
‘It Is a Pity’: China Could Stop the War but Leans Toward Russia, Zelensky Says
The report adds that Kyiv suffered the highest casualties with 31 killed and 106 injured, followed by cities in central and southern Ukraine, such as Kherson (25 killed; 334 injured), Kryvyi Rih (16 killed; 147 injured), and Zaporizhzhia (11 killed; 131 injured).
Totals for eastern Ukraine’s Kharkiv was not named in the list.
“Human safari”
Short-range drones, such as the first-person view (FPV) drones commonly used by frontline troops, are said to be the leading cause of frontline civilian deaths.
“Short-range drones were the main cause of civilian casualties near the frontline (91 killed; 727 injured), accounting for 30 percent of all civilian casualties in August,” it says.
While the report did not name specific frontline regions or cities affected by short-range drone strikes, southern Ukraine’s Kherson – sitting just across the river from Russian-occupied areas – has often been dubbed a “human safari” due to the prevalence of Russian FPV operators targeting civilians.
The city of Oleshky, sitting just across the river, is facing a humanitarian crisis as Russian forces have blocked off all routes in and out of the city with artillery and drones, allowing no aid to pass.
Ukraine’s human rights commissioner called the city a “death trap” on Wednesday and said Russia has refused to uphold a negotiated evacuation deal.
Read Kyiv Post’s August frontline report in Kherson here.
Unclear picture of Russian civilian casualties
The UN report says it verified 4 civilians killed and 35 injured in occupied territories, but
says it is unable to verify figures for civilians killed and injured in Russia.
“According to public statements by Russian authorities on individual incidents in August, at least 85 people were killed and 498 injured in occupied territory and at least 113 people killed and 736 injured in the Russian Federation,” the report says, before adding:
“Due to lack of independent sources of information, however, HRMMU has not been able to verify the vast majority of allegations.”

articles.title: Ukraine strikes two Russian S-400 launchers in Bryansk. The same systems were used to attack Kyiv overnight.
articles.body:
Ukrainian forces struck two Russian S-400 launchers in Russia’s Bryansk Oblast on 16–17 September, Ukraine’s General Staff reported. These same systems were used to launch missiles at Kyiv last night.
Ukraine faces severe shortages of high-end air-defense interceptors capable of countering Russia’s ballistic missiles, making strikes on the launchers themselves increasingly important. Russia has used S-400 systems to launch missiles at Ukrainian cities, including Kyiv, so destroying these systems can reduce Russia’s ability to carry out future attacks.
S-400 missile systems hit
The General Staff said Ukrainian Defense Forces struck two S-400 launchers near Vygonichi in Bryansk Oblast as part of a series of attacks on Russian military targets.
The strikes took place as Russia launched another major overnight attack against Ukraine. According to Ukraine’s Air Force, Russian forces used S-400, Iskander-M and KN-23 ballistic missiles launched from Bryansk and Voronezh oblasts, among other weapons.
The S-400 is a Russian long-range surface-to-air missile system designed to detect and engage aircraft and missiles. It was originally designed for air defense, but Russia has also used S-400 systems to launch ballistic missiles for strikes against Ukrainian cities, including Kyiv.
Kyiv Oblast was among the main targets of last night’s Russian attack.
One alternative to air defense: Ukraine strikes Russian Bastion system used to attack Ukrainian cities from Crimea
Ukraine targets Russian military infrastructure
The S-400 launchers were among several Russian military targets struck by Ukrainian forces on 16–17 September, the General Staff reported.
Near occupied Donetsk, Ukrainian forces hit a Russian site used to store, prepare, and launch attack drones. They also struck Russian logistics warehouses in Kurakhivka, Nova Mariivka, and Luhansk.
Ukrainian forces additionally hit Russian personnel concentration areas near Strilkove in occupied Kherson Oblast and Druzhne in occupied Luhansk Oblast.
The General Staff said operations against key Russian military targets are continuing.

articles.title: ‘Very Massive Explosion’: Russian Drone Falls 4 km From Poland
articles.body:
A jet-powered drone fell or was destroyed on Ukrainian territory about 4 kilometers (2.5 miles) from Poland during a Russian attack on western Ukraine on Thursday, Sept. 17, Polish officials said.
According to Polish outlet RMF24, Poland scrambled military aircraft and placed its air defenses on alert as the drone approached the NATO member’s border.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the explosion occurred near the Dorohusk crossing, close to a gas station on the Ukrainian side of the border.
“There was a very massive explosion. Our aircraft were scrambled,” Tusk said.
The blast was reported near Yahodyn, a Ukrainian settlement and major road and railway crossing opposite Dorohusk.
Polish authorities did not report that the drone had crossed into the country’s airspace. No information about casualties or the extent of the damage in Ukraine was immediately available.
Poland prepares to intercept drone
Polish Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk told parliament that the military was prepared to shoot down the drone if it approached Poland and posed a risk of crossing the border.
Polish military aircraft were deployed during the Russian attack, while warning sirens sounded in several eastern cities, including Lublin and Rzeszów.
Residents in central Poland also reported hearing a loud blast. The military said the sound came from Polish fighter jets breaking the sound barrier rather than an explosion on Polish territory.
Poland's Tusk to Visit Ukraine on Friday
Poland ended the military aviation operation and canceled its emergency alert after Russian strikes on western Ukraine had stopped.
Russia escalates attacks near NATO territory
The incident came during another widespread Russian missile and drone attack on Ukraine. Earlier on Thursday, civilian and energy infrastructure was damaged across eight regions, with at least 27 people injured in Kyiv and Odesa.
Russia has also recently intensified strikes against Ukrainian transport and logistics infrastructure close to the Polish border, including near a train carrying foreign diplomats and speakers after their attendance at Kyiv’s Yalta European Strategy (YES) conference.
The latest incident adds to mounting tensions between Moscow and Warsaw. On Tuesday, Sept. 15, senior Kremlin official Nikolai Patrushev threatened that Warsaw could “cease to exist” if Poland entered a military conflict with Russia.
Poland, a NATO and European Union member, has been one of Ukraine’s principal military and political supporters since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Quote: "There is a real risk that drones or other types of projectiles could be launched into the territory of one or several NATO countries on the eastern flank and could even cause damage, while the official version will be that it is an accident and that no one has reason to count on any response from NATO."

"The objective will be to undermine NATO's integrity as a whole and, above all, to convince member states that Article 5 is more theoretical than practical – that is, to proceed from the assumption that no one will want to die for Latvia or Lithuania, given that we are dealing with incidents rather than a declaration of war," the Polish prime minister added.

articles.title: Images reveal major damage to US bases from Iran strikes
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Images reveal major damage to US bases from Iran strikes
A destroyed aircraft, shredded tents, trailers that have been ripped apart: images taken by US troops show significant damage from Iranian strikes targeting American military assets in the Middle East, CBS News reported.
The undated images -- taken at a base in Saudi Arabia and two facilities in Kuwait -- were provided to CBS by American personnel on condition of anonymity due to US military restrictions, the outlet said late Tuesday.
"This is major damage to our bases that hasn't been communicated to the American public," CBS quoted one US service member as saying.
"We're standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face," the service member added.
The Pentagon's inspector general released a report earlier this week that said the military's Central Command (CENTCOM) -- which is responsible for US forces in the Middle East -- had reported widespread damage to American facilities and equipment.
CENTCOM said Iranian strikes "damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan," the report said.
"In addition, dozens of US aircraft were destroyed or damaged" during the war, the report said.
The Defense Department estimated the cost of the war at $33.4 billion as of June 29, but that figure "does not include costs for infrastructure repairs," according to the report.
The US and Israel launched the war on Iran on February 28, with President Donald Trump saying the goal was to prevent the Islamic republic from obtaining nuclear weapons -- which Tehran denies it is seeking.
Iran retaliated with attacks across the region and blockaded the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of world oil supplies previously flowed -- a move that has sent oil prices soaring and caused global economic fallout.

Both Russia and Ukraine have increased their use of long-range missiles in recent months, along with the continued use of drones, to strike inside each other's territories.
Mediated talks ahead?

Earlier this week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's office said officials were preparing for talks in October. Similar signals came from Moscow, which said it did not rule out such a possibility.

articles.title: China could acquire F-35 fighter jet technology through Saudi Arabia, US officials warn - report
articles.body:
US intelligence officers have voiced concerns that China could acquire F-35 fighter jet technology through Saudi Arabia, officials told The New York Times on Wednesday.
The officials' fears stem from the United States' multi-billion-dollar sale of 48 of the aircraft to Saudi Arabia, which has been pending since November 2025. Similar concerns were raised at the time the potential deal was initially announced.
The US officials said that China could receive the technology either via spying or through its military and security partnership with Saudi Arabia.
A Pentagon intelligence report on the subject, the NYT reported, said that the F-35 technology storage sites should be restricted to US and Saudi personnel.
Analysts in the report questioned whether Saudi Arabia would agree to limiting general contact with the Chinese military and associated entities, as well as removing equipment from Chinese manufacturers from telecommunications and router infrastructure.
The State Department, Pentagon, and Saudi Arabian Embassy in Washington declined to comment to the NYT, while the White House and Chinese Embassy did not reply to requests.
Saudi F-35 deal raises concerns over Israel's military edge
When the deal was first under consideration in 2025, the NYT reported that it had raised concerns over Israel’s qualitative military edge in the region.
Israel is the only country in the Middle East that currently operates these jets, using them in airstrikes on Iran in October 2024 and June 2025.
Since the 1973 war, US policymakers have worked to ensure that Israel maintains its qualitative military edge, with Congress requiring that the US guarantee Israel can defeat any “credible conventional military threat” while suffering minimal damage and casualties.
Eli Leon contributed to this report.

articles.title: RAF to fight above Britain in huge air defence exercise
articles.body:
The Royal Air Force has launched what it describes as the UK’s largest homeland defence air exercise, bringing together British and NATO aircraft for nearly three weeks of training focused on defending the UK and fighting alongside allies in a major conflict, according to the RAF.
Exercise Cobra Warrior 26-2 runs from 14 September to 2 October and involves personnel, aircraft and command-and-control specialists from the UK, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and the United States. The exercise is intended to test how quickly allied forces can integrate, operate from British bases, sustain complex missions and fight in contested airspace as part of a NATO force.
Chief of the Air Staff Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth said: “The return of great power competition across the globe and the significant, and growing, threat posed by Russia to the UK and NATO makes this, by far, the most dangerous period in my 35 years of military service.”
He added: “This is why the RAF is investing in our People and our capabilities – to defend the UK, deter our adversaries and, if necessary, defeat them across the Air and Space domains.”
Smyth said Cobra Warrior was being used to rehearse how the RAF would respond to aggression alongside its allies. He said: “Cobra Warrior gives us the opportunity to practise our response to aggression, ensuring we are testing our defences and ability to operate alongside NATO partners during a real conflict.”
The RAF contribution includes Typhoon and F-35 Lightning combat aircraft, P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft and aircraft from the Air Mobility Force, including Voyager tankers. They are operating alongside Italian and German Eurofighter Typhoons, US Air Force F-15, F-16 and F-35 aircraft, NATO E-3A airborne warning and control aircraft and KC-135 tankers.
The mix gives the exercise a broad air combat and support element, combining fighters with surveillance, maritime patrol, airborne warning and control and air-to-air refuelling aircraft. Cobra Warrior is also being used to test the RAF’s ability to protect and continue operating from its home bases while integrating allied forces at speed, a central part of the service’s Warfighting Ready and NATO First priorities.
The exercise marks the culmination of the UK Qualified Weapons Instructor courses, the RAF’s highest-level post-graduate warfighting qualification. Crews are being put through complex tactical scenarios intended to test planning, command and control and the execution of large multinational missions.
Italian personnel are operating from RAF Waddington during the exercise.
Italian Deployment Commander Major Valerio C said: “We are truly honoured and excited to be here at RAF Waddington to train alongside our NATO allies and international partners. Cobra Warrior represents the premier tactical training environment, offering an invaluable opportunity to enhance our interoperability, refine joint tactics, and strengthen our collective readiness.”
He added: “Participating with our aircraft and personnel allows us to test our capabilities in complex, contested and high-threat operational scenarios. The integration and shared expertise between our nations are what make the Alliance so strong. We look forward to a productive exercise and to flying shoulder-to-shoulder with our partners and qualifying Weapons Instructors.”
German Air Force personnel are meanwhile operating from RAF Cranwell, where the RAF says the deployment is being used to strengthen the relationships needed for allied forces to operate together during crisis or conflict.
RAF Cranwell Station Commander Wing Commander Mathew Thornton said: “RAF Cranwell is delighted to welcome our German Air Force colleagues to the Station for Exercise Cobra Warrior. This Exercise provides an opportunity to strengthen our long-standing professional relationships, train alongside one another and build lasting friendships.”
He added: “Visits such as these are invaluable and we are incredibly proud to welcome them to RAF Cranwell.”
Cobra Warrior brings together combat air, maritime patrol, air mobility, air-to-air refuelling, command and control and multi-domain activity within a single large-scale exercise, with the RAF using the event to test both homeland defence and the ability to operate as part of a NATO force in a high-threat environment.

articles.title: A six-fingered Leonardo DiCaprio and the creature from Ridley Scott’s ‘Alien’ stuff a ballot box in this Russian PSA about AI-generated election fraud videos
articles.body:
A six-fingered Leonardo DiCaprio and the creature from Ridley Scott’s ‘Alien’ stuff a ballot box in this Russian PSA about AI-generated election fraud videos
The Telegram channel Voyna s Feykami posted an AI-generated video about ballot stuffing. It shows a six-fingered Leonardo DiCaprio, soccer player Cristiano Ronaldo, and the alien from Ridley Scott’s film “Alien” dropping ballots into a ballot box. A voice-over warns that videos purporting to show election violations may have been generated using AI.
“Stay alert! In the coming days, as the election approaches, pressure on Russians will mount. Don’t believe everything you see online,” the channel says in the post accompanying the video. The channel urges readers to rely “only on official sources” for information about the election.
By the time this article was published, the video featuring DiCaprio had been viewed more than 100,000 times and shared by several other Telegram channels.
Russians lost real elections a long ago. But you’ve still got a choice. If you live outside Russia, please donate to Meduza — for yourself or for those who remain inside the country and want to read independent news.
Voyna s Feykami is run by Dialog, an autonomous nonprofit organization established by the Moscow authorities in 2019 as an online “citizen feedback” center. As Proekt reported, Dialog was actually tasked with promoting political advertising ahead of the vote on constitutional amendments. During the pandemic, Dialog was also responsible for providing information about the coronavirus. After Russia criminalized spreading false information about the virus, the organization began searching for such content.
The organization’s responsibilities expanded after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Dialog employees handled communications for the Defense Ministry and also fabricated stories about Ukraine. During this period, Dialog launched the Voyna s Feykami Telegram channel and a website of the same name.
In 2023, Meduza, iStories, and The Bell published a joint investigation into Dialog’s work. We found that Sergei Kiriyenko, the first deputy chief of staff of Russia’s Presidential Administration, oversees the organization on the Kremlin’s behalf. Sources described Vladimir Tabak, who has headed Dialog since 2021, as “Surkov’s man,” whom Kiriyenko had “inherited” along with his position. According to the sources, Kiriyenko personally visited the organization’s office to celebrate their victory in the vote on the constitutional amendments.
The journalists also examined Dialog’s internal guidelines for “debunking fake news.” When there is no basis whatsoever for refuting a story, the guidelines instruct employees to discredit the source, point out that the report contains no photos or videos, or suggest who might benefit from spreading it.
Voyna s Feykami has claimed, for example, that Ukrainian air defenses caused a gas explosion — not a Russian missile strike — that killed 46 people in an apartment building in Dnipro. It also described the strike that killed 12 people at a pizzeria in Kramatorsk as an attack on “a deployment site for foreign mercenaries.”

articles.title: Meduza found Russia’s unpublished anti-extremism plan on a school website. It calls for identifying ‘Russophobes’ in the military and using AI for propaganda.
articles.body:
Meduza found Russia’s unpublished anti-extremism plan on a school website. It calls for identifying ‘Russophobes’ in the military and using AI for propaganda.
Meduza found a publicly accessible copy of the unpublished “Action Plan for Implementing the Russian Federation’s Strategy for Countering Extremism.” Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Chernyshenko approved the plan in March 2025. The document was never officially published, but the authors of related regional and municipal plans cited a draft with the same title and reference number (No. DCh-P44-10219).
Vladimir Putin approved the strategy itself in December 2024. It details what the Kremlin considers the main “extremist” threats and how it intends to combat them. The action plan spells out the authorities’ next steps. But Meduza found that it sometimes goes far beyond the original document.
We found the plan in an unexpected place. The file, marked “for official use only,” appeared six months ago on the website of a school in the village of Leningradskaya, in Russia’s Krasnodar Krai, hosted on the gosuslugi.ru domain. On March 10–11, roughly a dozen other documents were uploaded to the same site. They included both the school’s internal plan for preventing extremism and terrorism and a comprehensive federal plan for countering terrorist ideology in 2024–2028. The latter was drafted by the head of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) and approved by the Russian president. It had been published before, but the school had a version bearing the signatures of Alexander Bortnikov and Vladimir Putin.
Is this document authentic?
Circumstantial evidence suggests the document is probably authentic, though we cannot be completely certain.
In theory, the electronic signature could be used to verify its authenticity, and there was reason to hope this would be possible. The first page bears a stamp reading, “Document signed electronically.” It also lists the signature’s identifier (00BC60EF36970905F3079D8DDD28705EBF), its validity period (April 23, 2024, to July 17, 2025), and its holder (Dmitry Chernyshenko). However, we do not know how to locate the signature itself.
For comparison, extracts from Russia’s Unified State Register of Legal Entities bear a similar notation, but their signatures are embedded in the files. The document we examined contains no embedded signature, though it could theoretically be stored in a separate external file. If you understand the intricacies of Russian government document management, please write to us.
We did, however, find an identical stamp with the same holder, identifier, and validity period in a government-issued assignment for Moscow State University published on the university’s website.
The federal plan we examined contains 77 items, each identifying the agencies responsible for that measure. The document does not describe in detail the steps proposed to implement the updated strategy for countering extremism, so the context of some initiatives may not be entirely clear. But the authorities appear to have identified specific phenomena and challenges they intend to tackle first, rather than abstract threats. Here is a look at the dangers the Kremlin sees — and where.
Russophobia was declared a new threat, but officials plan to look for it only in the military and security agencies
20. Taking measures to prevent and suppress Russophobia, xenophobia, radicalism, and extremism among military personnel and civilian staff of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation, the National Guard of the Russian Federation, the Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation, and the Interior Ministry of the Russian Federation.
The strategy for countering extremism defined Russophobia as follows:
An unfriendly, prejudiced, or hostile attitude toward Russian citizens, the Russian language and culture, and Russian traditions and history, expressed, among other things, in the aggressive attitudes and actions of political forces and their individual representatives, as well as discriminatory actions by the authorities of unfriendly states against Russia;
The strategy also linked Russophobia to the war in Ukraine. Putin accused unfriendly states of using the “Ukraine crisis” to “stoke aggressive Russophobic sentiment around the world.”
But judging by the action plan Meduza examined, one of the following must be true:
- Either Russophobia has been found only within the Defense Ministry, the National Guard, the FSB, and the Interior Ministry
- Or combating other Russophobes is much harder, if not impossible
- Or the federal authorities do not actually consider this fight a priority
Officials plan to look specifically for extremists among conscripts and contract soldiers
21. Taking joint measures, including through military enlistment offices and contract-service recruitment centers, to gather information on whether draft-age citizens and people signing military contracts are involved in the activities of extremist organizations.
The Defense Ministry, the National Guard, the Interior Ministry, and the FSB were assigned this task.
The strategy itself makes no mention of conscripts, contract soldiers, military enlistment offices, or even the Defense Ministry.
And among sports coaches, too
6. Taking legislative measures to prevent adherents of extremist ideology from infiltrating the sports sector, including the coaching and teaching staffs of sports schools and clubs.
The strategy describes a similar problem but focuses on combat sports:
The spread of radicalism in the sports community, including in sports schools and combat sports clubs, as well as the infiltration of coaching and instructional staff by adherents of extremist ideology, is a serious cause for concern.
The new wording could formally apply to every kind of sports school, including figure skating and chess schools.
In December 2025, it emerged that the authorities planned to create a single registry of coaches. Putin instructed the government to determine how the Sports Ministry would compile the registry, who would have access to the information, and how that access would work. The government had until April 15, 2026, to complete the task. It is unclear whether the cabinet met the deadline: no documents concerning the system’s launch are publicly available.
We do not know whether this initiative is related to the anti-extremism action plan. But we found no other “legislative measures.”
Ethnic and religious organized crime groups have apparently managed to corrupt parts of the government
13. Identifying and disrupting corrupt ties between organized criminal groups, including those formed along ethnic and religious lines, and state or local government bodies, and preventing these groups from financing extremist activity.
The strategy itself makes no mention of corruption or organized criminal groups — much less groups formed “along ethnic and religious lines.” It is unclear which religions this refers to. The law “On Freedom of Conscience and Religious Associations” lists only the following religions as forming “an integral part of the historical heritage of the peoples of Russia”:
- Christianity
- Islam
- Buddhism
- Judaism
Enemy number one Russia’s new national security strategy faces off against the US and threats to ‘spiritual values’
Further reading
The authorities believe residents of Ukraine’s occupied territories lack “traditional” Russian values
61. Taking measures to promote the smooth social and cultural integration into Russian society of residents of the Donetsk and Luhansk people’s republics and the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions, as well as people who have moved permanently from these territories to other regions of Russia, in order to prevent the social and political situation from deteriorating. Involving them in volunteer work and other activities that benefit society to instill in them traditional Russian spiritual and moral values.
The strategy itself already called for integrating residents of the occupied parts of Ukraine’s Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson regions. But the action plan indicates that they lack “traditional Russian spiritual and moral values” — values that still have to be instilled in them. A presidential decree issued in November 2022 established the following list of traditional values:
- Life
- Dignity
- Human rights and freedoms
- Patriotism
- Civic-mindedness
- Service to the Fatherland and responsibility for its fate
- High moral ideals
- Strong families
- Productive work
- The primacy of the spiritual over the material
- Humanism
- Compassion
- Justice
- Collectivism
- Mutual assistance and mutual respect
- Historical memory and continuity between generations
- The unity of Russia’s peoples
So what do they have instead of these values? Of course, the authorities did not forget about “neo-Nazism and Ukrainian nationalism”
12. Ensuring cooperation among entities involved in countering extremism in border territories and the territories of the Russian Federation’s new constituent regions in order to prevent members of international extremist and terrorist organizations from entering the Russian Federation. Implementing coordinated measures aimed at preventing and suppressing the spread of extremist ideology in the new constituent regions of the Russian Federation, primarily neo-Nazism and Ukrainian nationalism.
The plan envisioned using AI for anti-extremism propaganda
45. Developing proposals for using artificial intelligence and big-data processing technologies to monitor media outlets and information and telecommunications networks, including the Internet; conduct streaming data analysis; identify anonymous participants in extremist activity; and prepare and distribute informational materials on preventing and suppressing extremist activity, with the aim of making Russian citizens more vigilant and encouraging them to take an interest in countering extremism.
The strategy itself already mentioned plans to use artificial intelligence to identify anonymous “extremists” and monitor publications. The plan retained this wording verbatim but added plans to use AI for propaganda. It is unclear exactly what the Digital Development Ministry, the federal media regulator Roskomnadzor, the Interior Ministry, and the FSB were being asked to do. The first thing that comes to mind is generating AI slop for social media.

articles.title: Democrats' Israel divide widens in House Foreign Affairs
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
The Democrats' divide over Israel comes to the House Foreign Affairs Committee
Washington, DC - On August 25, 2026, US Representative Jared Moskowitz (D-FL) was selected by the Democratic Party to become the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee’s (HFAC) Subcommittee on the Middle East and North Africa.
The appointment comes at a moment when many Democratic voters are increasingly critical of US policies toward Israel, Gaza, Iran, and the broader region.
If Democrats regain control of the House after the November 2026 midterm elections, the party would be putting one of its staunchest pro-Israel members in line to chair the powerful subcommittee despite opposition from their own base.
Moskowitz comes to the post with several years of experience on HFAC. During the 119th Congress, he has served as the ranking member of the Subcommittee on Oversight and Intelligence, where he has played a prominent role in congressional scrutiny of the Department of State and the larger US foreign policy apparatus.
Moskowitz has been prominent in his ardent support for Israel. He has notably championed legislation to strengthen US–Israeli defence cooperation and has been among the party’s most vocal advocates for the Abraham Accords, introducing bipartisan legislation in 2025 that would expedite certain arms sales to countries that have normalised relations with Israel and that cooperate with the United States against Iran and Iranian-backed groups.
In the same spirit, Moskowitz has also collaborated with Republicans to stymie international pressure on Israel. He was one of just 16 House Democrats to join Republicans in voting for legislation seeking to force former President Joe Biden to release a shipment of bombs to Israel and has worked closely with Republican Congressman Mike Lawler (R-NY) to halt US funding to UN agencies that expel or restrict Israel.
Moskowitz’s appointment also hands the Democratic Party’s Middle East portfolio to one of its more hawkish voices on Iran. Moskowitz has positioned himself to the right of Vice President JD Vance and Special Envoy Steve Witkoff on Iran policy, saying that his views align more closely with Sen. Tom Cotton (R-AR) and the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-SC), two of the Senate’s most prominent Iran hawks.
Both senators have defended using military force against Iran, and Graham credited himself with persuading President Trump to go to war.
Moskowitz also initially opposed the Iran War Powers Resolution introduced by Reps. Ro Khanna (D-CA) and Thomas Massie (R-KY) to restrain Trump from escalating against Iran, calling the measure the “Ayatollah Protection Act” and putting himself at odds with most of his own party and its leadership.
He ultimately voted for the resolution once the US strikes had begun but framed his support as a defence of Congress’s war powers rather than opposition to the war.
On the domestic front, Moskowitz has built a political record around delegitimising pro-Palestine activism. In April 2025, he reintroduced legislation that would prevent the federal government from contracting with entities that participate in the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement, declaring that BDS “has no place in federal contracts” and characterising the entire movement as antisemitic.
Moskowitz has likewise been critical of the university campus movements for Palestine. At the height of the 2024 university protests, he became a vocal critic of such student activism in Congress.
His subsequent legislative agenda has reinforced that position. In February 2025, the Florida representative backed the Antisemitism Awareness Act, which would require the Department of Education to use the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s (IHRA) working definition when evaluating discrimination complaints, including examples concerning certain forms of criticism of Israel.
The IHRA definition conflates criticism of Israel and Zionism with antisemitism, which in practice chills free speech and punishes those who speak out against Israel and its violations of Palestinian rights, while undermining efforts to combat antisemitism itself.
In Florida’s August 18, 2026, Democratic primary, Moskowitz handily defeated his challenger, Oliver Larkin, a Democratic Socialist who had made opposition to US support for Israel a focal point of his campaign. Moskowitz won roughly 64 percent of the vote in the newly drawn 25th Congressional District, while Larkin received 36 percent.
Moskowitz’s victory, however, took place despite a broader change in Democratic voters’ attitudes toward Israel. In a May 2026 New York Times/Siena poll, 74 percent of potential Democratic supporters expressed opposition to sending additional US economic and military aid to Israel, up from 45 percent in December 2023.
The 2026 poll showed that 95 percent of potential Democratic voters opposed the US–Israeli war on Iran and nearly half said that their party was too supportive of Israel. In April 2026, Pew Research Center found that 80 percent of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents held an unfavourable view of Israel, compared with 53 percent in 2022.
An August 2026 poll by the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy (IMEU) Project revealed that most Democratic voters in the first six states to hold presidential primaries in 2028 - and in some cases, significant majorities - prefer a presidential candidate who supports sanctioning and cutting off US weapons transfers to Israel.
The shift on Israel is becoming increasingly visible among Democratic lawmakers as well. On July 15, 2026, 103 House Democrats voted for Rep. Thomas Massie’s (R-KY) amendment to eliminate $3.3 billion in annual US security assistance to Tel Aviv. By comparison, an April 2024 bill to provide additional military aid to Israel was opposed by just 37 Democratic lawmakers.
The same trend was reflected in the primary season, when several candidates running on more critical positions toward Israel prevailed in closely watched Democratic races. In Michigan, Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed won even after the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) and its allies spent more than $54 million against him. Wins like these would have been unlikely a few election cycles ago.
Still, the success of candidates openly critical of Israel has not pulled the Democratic establishment away from its longstanding support, even as some party leaders have modified their rhetoric toward the Israeli government ahead of the midterms. More importantly, many establishment politicians continue to take substantial campaign funding from AIPAC.
According to Track AIPAC, Moskowitz has received $833,288 in campaign contributions from pro-Israel groups over the course of his career and continues to maintain close ties to controversial lobbying groups.
Ultimately, these developments expose a widening gap on Israel between the Democratic establishment and its base. By elevating lawmakers like Moskowitz to influential foreign policy positions, party leaders are once again demonstrating how out of touch they are with popular sentiment.
As ranking member, Moskowitz could use his position to preserve and strengthen pro-Israel tendencies in the party, even as more Democratic voters and lawmakers move in the opposite direction.
