articles.title: Russia launched a massive overnight attack on Ukraine with missiles and 157 drones — air defenses neutralized 131 targets
articles.body:
Russia launched a massive overnight attack on Ukraine with missiles and 157 drones — air defenses neutralized 131 targets
Kyiv • UNN
Russia struck Ukraine with ballistic and cruise missiles and 157 drones. Air defenses neutralized 131 targets; strikes were recorded at 36 locations.
During the night of September 17, Russia launched a massive combined attack on Ukraine using ballistic and cruise missiles, Oniks missiles, as well as 157 attack and decoy drones. Air defense forces shot down or suppressed 131 aerial targets, the Ukrainian Air Force reported, according to UNN.
Details
The main targets of Russia’s strike were the Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia, and Odesa regions. The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, as well as mobile fire groups.
According to the Air Force, Russia used Oniks anti-ship missiles, Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles, 4 Kalibr cruise missiles, 10 Bandероль/Dan-T missiles, as well as 157 Shahed-type attack UAVs and decoy drones. More than half of the launched Shaheds were jet-powered.
Air defense neutralized 131 targets
As of 08:00, air defense had shot down or suppressed 7 Bandероль/Dan-T missiles and 124 Shahed-type, Gerbera, and other types of drones.
At the same time, missile and attack UAV strikes were recorded at 36 locations. At another 5 locations, the falls of downed targets or their fragments were recorded.
The Air Force emphasized that, as of the time the report was published, the attack was ongoing—several Russian drones remained in Ukraine’s airspace.

articles.title: US Congress approves Russia sanctions that impact China and India
articles.body:
US lawmakers have approved sweeping new sanctions targeting Russia's economy and Putin's inner circle, with Trump set to sign a bill that also threatens steep tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil, including China and India.
The US House of Representatives approved a major new package of sanctions against Russia on Wednesday, clearing the way for President Donald Trump to sign into law the most significant American legislative action against Moscow since he returned to the White House.
Lawmakers passed the measure 262 to 159, following the Senate's own overwhelming approval, 86 to 11, last month. Trump has indicated he will sign it.
The sanctions target Russia's energy and defence industries, President Vladimir Putin and senior officials around him, and the so-called "shadow fleet" of tankers Moscow uses to evade existing Western restrictions.
Crucially for global energy markets, the bill also grants Trump the power to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries that continue buying large volumes of Russian oil and gas — a measure aimed squarely at China and India, two of Moscow's biggest remaining customers.
That tariff provision proved contentious even among supporters of Ukraine in Washington. Some Democrats, while backing tougher action against Russia, objected to giving the president such broad authority over trade policy.
Gregory Meeks, the senior Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, criticised the bill's drafting, arguing it prioritised presidential tariff powers over binding sanctions commitments. He said he would have supported the legislation had the tariff measures been stripped out, but Republicans blocked attempts to amend them.
Despite these reservations, most Democrats ultimately voted for the bill, while a small number of Republicans opposed it on free-market grounds. Supporters say the added pressure is necessary as Russia's full-scale invasion enters its fifth year with no ceasefire in sight.
Kyiv welcomes the bill but India holds firm
The vote came as Russian drone strikes hit civilian transport in southern Ukraine on Wednesday, killing five people, according to officials in Kyiv — an attack that added urgency to calls from pro-Ukraine campaigners for the bill's passage.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had lobbied Congress directly to pass the sanctions, arguing that only sustained economic pressure would push Moscow toward negotiations. Speaking in Washington in July, he said Russia was losing around 30,000 soldiers a month but showed no sign of ending the war, adding that the initiative on the battlefield had shifted out of Putin's hands.
India responded on Thursday by signalling it would not change course, saying it would continue purchasing Russian oil "through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics."
Russia remains one of India's most important strategic and military partners, complicating Washington's efforts to isolate Moscow economically.
The legislation also targets companies and foreign entities supporting Russia's military effort and extends existing sanctions related to Iran. It follows more than a year of delay, reflecting Trump's general preference for retaining personal control over sanctions and tariff policy rather than ceding it to Congress.
Ukrainian advocacy groups welcomed the bill's passage while urging swift enforcement. "Once the bill is quickly signed and becomes law, we hope for strong US enforcement to finally end the cash flows to the Kremlin's war chest," said Svitlana Romanko of the energy lobby group Razom We Stand.
"Every day of delay is a day we in Ukraine must bury more people."

articles.title: Zelenskyy seeks drone deal, closer defense technology ties with Japan
articles.body:
Elena Teslova
17 September 2026•Update: 17 September 2026
Ukraine wants to expand defense technology cooperation with Japan, including through a proposed drone deal, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Thursday.
In an interview with Japanese broadcaster NHK, Zelenskyy said Japanese companies could benefit from Ukraine’s experience in maritime monitoring, reconnaissance, mine clearance, air defense and cybersecurity.
“We very much want to build military-technology cooperation between Ukraine and Japan,” he said, expressing interest in partnerships at both government and business levels.
More than 70% of Ukraine’s defense industry was in the private sector, he said, suggesting that closer defense ties could also boost bilateral trade. Any decisions on defense equipment would be up to Japan, he added.
Zelenskyy said cooperation could contribute to security in the Asia-Pacific region, warning that North Korea was gaining combat experience through its military involvement in Russia.
He alleged that Pyongyang had sent between 30,000 and 50,000 troops to Russia, where they had gained experience in modern warfare, including drone operations, that could later be applied elsewhere.
Turning to China, Zelenskyy accused Beijing of failing to use its influence over Moscow to help end the war.
“I don’t see China putting pressure on Russia to stop the war,” he said.
He described himself as “vexed” by China’s lack of political support for Ukraine and said Beijing was “a little bit more” on Russia’s side.
Zelenskyy said he had not personally seen Chinese-made missiles in Ukraine. While alleging that Chinese equipment and technology were reaching Russia, he clarified that he was not referring to direct Chinese weapons supplies.
China has said it is not a party to the conflict and has called for a political settlement.

articles.title: Pentagon wants new mobile radar to track hypersonic weapons
articles.body:
The Missile Defense Agency wants industry to build a new mobile radar that can be flown into a war zone aboard a C-17, set up within hours and torn down again in minutes, according to a pre-solicitation notice posted September 16.
The program, called Forward Based Mode Radar Next, is meant to replace or supplement current forward-deployed missile-tracking radars with a system that can move fast enough to survive against an adversary trying to target it. The notice comes from the agency’s Mobile Land-Based Sensors Project Office and lays out plans to run the effort through NOBLE, the Missile Defense Agency’s existing Other Transaction Authority vehicle for prototype work.
The radar’s job is to provide early warning and tracking against ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and hypersonic weapons, then feed that data into the wider missile defense network. The agency says current forward-based radars are largely static or only semi-mobile, which makes them vulnerable to counterattack and slow to reposition as a fight evolves.
FBM Radar Next is meant to close that gap. Beyond fitting inside a C-17 and tactical ground vehicles, the notice calls for a design that can run with a minimal onsite crew, monitor its own health automatically, and reconfigure itself as either one large radar array or several smaller ones spread across a wider area. The agency also wants the system engineered to keep its physical, thermal and electromagnetic signatures low enough to avoid being easily targeted once deployed.
Cost is a central requirement rather than an afterthought. The notice specifically asks companies to show a path to high-volume, affordable production, framing the radar as something the military may need to replace quickly and repeatedly in a heavily contested environment rather than field as a small number of exquisite, expensive units.
Before any company can compete for the program, it has to clear what the agency calls an Entry Gate. That requires showing a fully documented subarray design and working hardware at the array element level, backed by real test data on things like transceiver performance and signal path continuity. Purely theoretical designs or software simulations without hardware behind them will not qualify.
Companies that clear the Entry Gate then move through four prototyping cycles, each ending in a competitive down-select. Cycle 1 covers concept development, Cycle 2 focuses on manufacturing readiness, Cycle 3 calls for a subscale prototype paired with modeling and simulation, and Cycle 4 culminates in a full-scale prototype and operational demonstration. The agency has not set specific timelines for any of the cycles, and no cost or contract value has been disclosed.
The Missile Defense Agency also flagged that only companies that complete the prototype effort will be eligible for what it describes as a likely sole-source follow-on production contract, and offerors will need to obtain a Facility Security Clearance before starting Cycle 1.
The agency stressed that the September 16 notice is not a request for proposals and does not commit it to a formal solicitation. It said it is not currently accepting questions or feedback on the notice, and a timeline for issuing an actual solicitation has not been announced.

articles.title: From ‘city of camels’ to Israel’s new dream: Beersheba reinventing itself under Mayor Danilovich
articles.body:
“When I was a child in Beersheba, between Beersheba and Tel Aviv it was like light-years,” the mayor told The Jerusalem Post. “They called us the city of camels, the end of the world, a desert city.”
Danilovich, born in Beersheba in 1971 and mayor since 2008, has spent much of his political life trying to dismantle that image. Today, the city has around 223,600 residents and some 30,000 students studying at its higher-education institutions. Ben-Gurion University of the Negev alone has around 20,000 students and says roughly a third of Israel’s engineers graduate from BGU.
Those numbers help explain why Danilovich’s enthusiastic outlook on his hometown suggests a place seen less as Israel’s periphery and more as a place where several of the country’s largest national projects are now converging.
The IDF began moving units into its new technological campus in Beersheba in May, next to the Gav-Yam Negev high-tech park and close to BGU. Around 8,000 soldiers and career officers are ultimately expected to serve there. Northeast of the city, the Intelligence Campus near Shoket Junction is being built for well over 10,000 Intelligence Directorate personnel.
Across the road from the university, Gav-Yam says some 2,500 engineers already work for around 70 companies at its Beersheba technology park. Nvidia, meanwhile, has been expanding its presence in the city, tripling its office space and planning to recruit hundreds of employees.
Beersheba’s tech ecosystem draws global companies
“The companies come by themselves,” Danilovich said. “They are not philanthropic. They are business companies. They come where it is worthwhile for them.”
He reeled off Microsoft, Dell, Nvidia, IBM and Deutsche Telekom before turning to the geography itself: the university, Soroka University Medical Center, the National Cyber Directorate, military technology units and defense companies, all clustered within a relatively small area.
“Show me another city – not in Israel, in the world – where in such a small radius there is such a concentration of knowledge,” he said.
That concentration is at the heart of what Danilovich repeatedly calls the “new Israeli dream.” The Negev accounts for around 60% of Israel’s territory and is home to roughly 1.5 million people. He argues that successive governments have allowed too much of the country’s population and economic activity to remain concentrated in the center, while neglecting the South's sheer size and potential.
“The Negev is not the problem of the State of Israel,” he told the Post. “The Negev can be the solution.”
Beersheba mayor looks to aliyah to reshape Israel’s periphery
Aliyah is central to that proposal. Danilovich wants Israel to set a national target of one million new immigrants over five to seven years, paired with housing incentives, employment, and community infrastructure intended to encourage many to settle in the Negev and Galilee.
Beersheba has precedent for immigration changing the character of the city. More than 60,000 immigrants from the former Soviet Union arrived during the great aliyah wave of the 1990s, bringing doctors, engineers, academics, and a substantial new Russian-speaking community to Beersheba. Danilovich points particularly to Soroka, where some of the young immigrant physicians who arrived then would later rise to head hospital departments.
“When did we become the Start-Up Nation?” Danilovich asked. “When the gates of the former Soviet Union opened.”
Since October 7, he has also framed his aliyah drive around the rise in antisemitism abroad, particularly in countries such as Britain, France and Canada. His complaint is that while Israel has mechanisms for absorbing newcomers, it lacks the kind of large-scale national plan that could take advantage of a major new wave of immigration if one materialized.
“Come home,” he said. “We will receive you with open arms.”
Another part of that thinking is already taking shape in Beersheba. JNF-USA is developing a $350 million World Zionist Village in the city, whose master plan was approved in 2025. The organization now expects it to open in 2029, with plans for educational programs, accommodation and a center intended to bring young Jews and community leaders from around the world to spend meaningful periods of time in Israel.
Danilovich hopes some will stay. He is almost as interested, however, in those who eventually return to London, Toronto, Johannesburg, Melbourne or elsewhere after a year spent in Beersheba.
“Maybe you will want to make aliyah,” he said. “And even if you don’t, you will go back... but you will be a good ambassador for the State of Israel.”
War leaves its mark on Beersheba’s growth
Beersheba’s development has taken place alongside a less welcome constant: war. Soroka, the main hospital serving southern Israel, took a direct hit from an Iranian ballistic missile on June 19, 2025. The government subsequently approved NIS 360 million toward reconstruction, while philanthropist Sylvan Adams pledged another $100 million.
For Danilovich, the cranes that will rise at Soroka are something he has been through before. He was in his mid-30s when he defeated veteran mayor Yaakov Turner in the November 2008 election, after already serving a decade as deputy mayor. Within weeks, Beersheba was under rocket fire from Gaza during Operation Cast Lead.
Since then, he has led the city through repeated rounds of fighting, each followed, in his memory, by the return of construction.
“After every round ended, I would see the cranes in Beersheba,” he recalled. “Suddenly we are building another neighborhood, suddenly the lake, suddenly the amphitheater, suddenly the high-tech park, suddenly the stadium. We don’t stop for a moment.”
The physical change is obvious to anyone who remembers the older city. Beersheba River Park occupies land where sewage, rubbish and industrial waste once lined the banks of Nahal Beersheba; the rehabilitation project now stretches for kilometers through the city.
From football stadium to high tech, Danilovich eyes the next stage
Danilovich has his own, rather less grandiose benchmark. A former amateur football player, he remembers Beersheba’s old stadium as so uninviting that women and children rarely attended, and even decent toilets were a problem.
Today, he can list the stadium alongside the high-tech park, university, cultural institutions and national park River Park when describing how far his hometown has traveled. Yet after nearly 18 years as mayor, he is wary of sounding satisfied.
“A mayor who is satisfied is not a serious mayor,” Danilovich told the Post. “A mayor should never be satisfied, because he always has to aspire to the next thing.”
Danilovich has received many offers over the years to make the move into national politics, including approaches from prime ministers and other political leaders. He said he turned them down.
“My mission for the State of Israel, for my people and for my country is here,” he said. “It is in the Negev.
“If we do not make it flourish, if we do not strengthen it, if we do not build it and make it attractive, if it does not become the new Israeli dream, the State of Israel will be in danger.”

articles.title: Fire temporarily shuts part of Slovak ammunition plant amid plans to triple capacity
articles.body:
ZVS Holding evacuated its ammunition factory in Snina, a town in eastern Slovakia, on 16 September after a fire broke out on the roof of a production building. Work stopped temporarily in the affected section, but nobody was injured, Militarnyi reported.
The Snina plant has an annual capacity of roughly 100,000 shells and plans to triple it, Noviny reported. The blaze briefly disrupted part of a facility under expansion for Europe’s ammunition buildup, although co-owner CSG expects no impact on customer deliveries. Authorities across Europe are investigating suspected Russian sabotage against defense companies, but no evidence links the Snina fire to that campaign.
ZVS Holding is owned equally by the Slovak state and the Czech defense conglomerate Czechoslovak Group (CSG). It makes 155 mm artillery shells, 120 mm tank rounds, and 30/35 mm cannon ammunition.
In December 2025, ZVS signed a seven-year framework agreement with Slovakia’s Defense Ministry to supply EU states. Purchases under the agreement may be financed through the bloc’s SAFE defense-loan program. Its Euro 58 billion ceiling represents the maximum possible value of future orders, not guaranteed purchases.
Firefighters brought the blaze under control during the afternoon. As thick black smoke rose over Snina, town officials advised nearby residents to limit time outdoors, close windows and doors, and switch off ventilation systems drawing in outside air.
Slovak Defense Minister Robert Kaliňák said the fire had not reached the plant’s production equipment and that the affected part of the building was not being used for manufacturing at the time. That section makes metal projectiles, he said.
Kaliňák said welding during the renovation may have sparked the fire, but stressed that investigators had not established the cause.
CSG said the fire started during roof repairs conducted by an external contractor. The company said the damage and cause still had to be assessed, but it did not expect the incident to affect customer deliveries, STVR reported.
Why sabotage fears shadow Europe’s arms plants
The Snina blaze was at least the fourth fire or explosion at a European ammunition facility since 10 August, after two fires struck a Bulgarian company and an explosion hit an Italian factory. No common cause has been established.
Preliminary findings pointed away from outside interference in the first Bulgarian fire. No evidence of sabotage, however, was reported after the Italian blast, and only the second Bulgarian fire remains under investigation for possible sabotage.
Czech authorities are examining a possible Russian trail behind an arson attack on a factory making drones and thermal optics for Ukraine.
Estonia has also probed suspected arson at a military-robot maker after courts documented earlier attacks directed by Russian military intelligence.

articles.title: US Congress passes Russia sanctions bill
articles.body:
US Congress passes Russia sanctions bill
September 17, 2026
The US Republican-led US House of Representatives passed on Wednesday a package of broad new sanctions against Russia over its war in Ukraine.
The bill passed 262-159, after breezing through the Senate in an 86-11 vote last month.
The bill, considered the toughest legislative effort against Russia during US President Donald Trump's second term, awaits the president's signature to come into law. Trump has said he will sign it.
What does the sanctions package against Russia entail?
The package targets Russia's energy and defense sectors, President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials. It also targets Moscow's so-called shadow fleet, old tankers it uses to circumvent sanctions.
More controversially, the legislation allows Trump to impose secondary sanctions on countries that rely on Russian oil and gas, in the form of tariffs. China and India are expected to be the main targets of such measures.
The bill would also extend sanctions on Iran.
It was drafted in April 2025 by late Republican senator Lindsey Graham, who died suddenly in July.
But Trump had delayed the bill's passage, as his foreign policy favors retaining control over tariffs and sanctions rather than leaving such decisions to Congress.
Who opposed the bill and why?
Democrats who voted for the bill broke ranks with the party leadership, which argues the legislation expands Trump's tariff powers and that the president already has the power to sanction Russia should he choose to.
"What this legislation will do is give Donald Trump, perhaps, unfettered authority to unleash tariffs on the American people," House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said in a speech on Wednesday.
Meanwhile, some Republicans opposed to the bill were wary of compounded tariffs further increasing consumer prices ahead of the midterm elections in November.
The bill's supporters say it is integral to keeping up the pressure on Russia.
It has been celebrated by Ukrainian activists. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with lawmakers to urge its passage and even watched an early procedural vote from the chamber.

articles.title: The EU has billions in unspent defense funds. It wants to use them for projects with Ukraine
articles.body:
The EU plans to use money remaining under its €150 billion Security Action for Europe (SAFE) program to create a new program for joint projects with Ukrainian companies, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on 16 September. She announced the plan during her State of the Union address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg.
Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine has pushed the EU to spend more on defense and build up its own weapons industry. SAFE was created as part of that effort, giving EU member states €150 billion in loans for defense spending. Ukraine is also facing heavy defense costs, with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy putting its additional defense funding gap for 2026 at $27 billion.
"Using the remaining funds from SAFE, we will be setting up a new programme for joint projects with Ukrainian companies," von der Leyen told the European Parliament.
EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius estimated that the unused portion of SAFE could amount to €10 billion to €20 billion, UNN reported. The exact sum will be known only after member states report on their SAFE projects by the end of October. The announcement caught several governments off guard: Poland and other capitals say the Commission never discussed it with them, and Warsaw had been counting on taking up the funds other countries declined for its own projects.
The proposal would allow unused money from member states' SAFE allocations to be redirected to joint projects with Ukrainian firms. One likely destination is Freya, the joint European-Ukrainian air and missile defense system meant as a cheaper answer to the American Patriot, which von der Leyen described as the start of the collaboration rather than the end of it.
In 2025, Ukraine gained associate partner status in SAFE and access to the EU's European Defense Fund, allowing Ukrainian companies to compete for contracts and co-develop military systems with European firms.
Fifteen member states have since said they plan to buy Ukrainian weapons through the program, and Canada joined it in December 2025 as the first non-European partner. Bulgaria agreed SAFE-funded joint weapons production with Ukraine in March 2026.
The war is costing Ukraine more every year, the government says. Its draft 2027 budget proposes ₴4.885 trillion ($110 billion) for defense needs, nearly 44% of GDP.

articles.title: ‘War without battle’: Europe struggles to tackle mounting Russian hybrid attacks
articles.body:
‘War without battle’: Europe struggles to tackle mounting Russian hybrid attacks
From sabotage and arson to cyberattacks and airspace violations, officials say Moscow’s hybrid actions have moved deeper into Europe
Over the course of the summer, Russian attacks have been pushing ever deeper into European territory.
On August 11, military divers destroyed two drones floating off the coast of Romania near a €4 billion (US$4.7 billion) energy project. Nine days later, Bucharest scrambled two F-16s to take out a maritime drone near the same Black Sea gas platform with hundreds of workers on board.
Earlier that month, German police detected an armed UAV at Leipzig airport, while this week Nato jets downed another unmanned aircraft that entered Lithuanian airspace from neighbouring Belarus, an ally of Moscow. In all these cases, the authorities pointed the finger squarely at the Kremlin.
As Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war on Ukraine grinds on with little movement on the battlefield and thousands of casualties each week, so-called hybrid attacks on Europe are increasing not just in number, but in their recklessness.

articles.title: EU ambassador on overnight attack: "Kyiv has become a frontline city"
articles.body:
EU ambassador on overnight attack: "Kyiv has become a frontline city"
EU Ambassador to Ukraine Katarína Mathernová has commented on the 17 September Russian attack on Ukrainian cities, including Kyiv.
Source: Mathernová on X (Twitter), as reported by European Pravda
Details: Mathernová said the death toll in the city of Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast alone since the beginning of August is approaching 120.
Quote: "Kyiv has become a frontline city. Since 27 August, we have had nighttime and daytime attacks. The Russians struck us heavily last night, with a massive combined missile & drone attack. The attack ended just a few minutes ago… Russia launched dozens of ballistic and cruise missiles and hundreds of drones, more than half of them jet-powered."
More details: Mathernová also commented on a Russian attack on a passenger train in Mykolaiv Oblast on 16 September. A total of 168 passengers and train attendants were evacuated because of the threat of further strikes.
Quote: "I love Ukrainian trains. I love travelling on them. Today I still do, but with fear."
More details: Mathernová pointed to Russia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs describing Ukraine's railway infrastructure as a "legitimate military target" and said no one could guarantee the safety of Western politicians and diplomats visiting Ukraine.
Quote: "That is not a warning. It is an admission."
Background:
- On the night of 16-17 September, Russia attacked Ukraine with 157 drones and anti-ship, ballistic and cruise missiles. Air defence forces have managed to down 131 aerial assets. The attack has injured 19 people, including two children, and damaged residential buildings, educational institutions, offices, a petrol station, warehouses, cars and railway infrastructure facilities.
- On 13 September, Russia attacked a locomotive near the Polish border. The state-run railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia (Ukrainian Railways) suggested that the intended target may have been a train carrying European diplomats, which had departed the station earlier than scheduled.

articles.title: Ukraine's Defence Intelligence reveals foreign equipment used by Russia to produce Geran drones
articles.body:
Ukraine's Defence Intelligence reveals foreign equipment used by Russia to produce Geran drones
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) has released data on 20 pieces of foreign technological equipment used to produce various modifications of Geran attack drones at the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Russia's Tatarstan, located about 1,200 km from the front line.

articles.title: While Ukraine lacks sufficient air defense missiles, the US used more than 4 interceptor missiles for each target during the attack on Iran
articles.body:
While Ukraine lacks sufficient air defense missiles, the US used more than 4 interceptor missiles for each target during the attack on Iran
Kyiv • UNN
The US launched approximately 82 Patriot and THAAD missiles, intercepting 18 of 20 Iranian ballistic missiles. Ukraine is forced to conserve PAC-3s.
The U.S. military used approximately 82 Patriot and THAAD interceptor missiles to intercept 20 Iranian ballistic missiles during the attack on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan on September 9. That averages more than four interceptors per target, while Ukraine, due to an ammunition shortage, is forced to use Patriot missiles much more sparingly, Defense Express reports, citing The Wall Street Journal, writes UNN.
Details
According to the publication, during the attack U.S. forces launched approximately 70 scarce PAC-3 missiles for Patriot systems. In addition, the THAAD missile defense system deployed approximately 12 more interceptors.
Despite the significant expenditure of ammunition, U.S. forces managed to intercept 18 of the 20 Iranian ballistic missiles. American military aircraft were also damaged in the strike.
Ukraine economizes on Patriot missiles
Defense Express notes that in Ukraine, due to a shortage of interceptors, only one Patriot missile per target may be used when intercepting ballistic targets.
The high expenditure of PAC-3 missiles by the U.S. military is also drawing attention because of the limited stocks of these missiles. This issue is particularly significant for Ukraine, as the PAC-3 is one of the key means of intercepting ballistic missiles.
The THAAD system was also used during the attack in Jordan. Iran had previously destroyed one of the AN/TPY-2 radar stations required for its operation, so, as Defense Express notes, the United States likely had to redeploy another such radar to the area of the air base.

articles.title: US House Passes Sweeping Russia Sanctions Bill, Sends It to Trump
articles.body:
The US House of Representatives passed a sweeping bipartisan sanctions and tariff package on Wednesday, giving President Donald Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian energy.
The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 passed by 262 votes to 159 and now heads to Trump’s desk. The Senate approved the measure 86-11 in August.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The legislation is aimed at cutting the financial and logistical networks that help Moscow sustain its war against Ukraine, targeting Russia’s energy sector, defense suppliers, major financial institutions and sanctions-evasion networks.
It also authorizes sanctions against individuals involved in the abduction of Ukrainian children.
Pressure on Russian energy revenues
At the center of the bill is a secondary-tariff mechanism aimed at countries continuing to buy Russian oil and gas.
President Trump would be able to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries purchasing large volumes of Russian energy or helping Moscow evade sanctions. Major buyers such as China and India could be affected, depending on how the measures are implemented.
Supporters say the goal is to reduce the flow of energy revenue that continues to finance Russia’s war.
Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal, who worked on the legislation with Graham, described the measures as “scorching sanctions” intended to “throttle Putin’s war machine.”
At Least 10 Explosions Rock Kyiv as Russian Attack Injures 12, Including Two Children
Banks, shadow fleet and military suppliers
The package also targets Russia’s so-called shadow fleet of oil tankers used to move crude despite Western restrictions.
It would sanction foreign suppliers supporting Russia’s defense sector, networks helping Moscow circumvent existing measures, and Russian officials and military figures.
New US investment in Russia would also face restrictions, along with exports that could support the Russian military.
Graham’s final sanctions push
The bill is named after the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, one of Washington’s most prominent supporters of Ukraine and a key architect of the sanctions push.
Graham spent more than a year building support for the legislation before his death in July.
The bill’s passage marks one of Congress’s most consequential recent moves to increase economic pressure on Moscow as Ukraine continues to resist Russia’s full-scale invasion.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia seeking support after US declines to strike Houthis – AP
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia seeking support after US declines to strike Houthis – AP
Saudi Arabia has turned to regional and global players for help defending its airspace against attacks from Yemen’s Houthi rebels after its main security provider, the US, declined to step in, The Associated Press has reported, citing regional officials. Riyadh is running low on missile interceptors, according to the outlet.
The armed conflict between a Saudi-led coalition and Houthi militants reignited in mid-July after Riyadh carried out airstrikes on the airport in Sanaa to prevent an Iranian passenger plane from landing there. In recent weeks, the Houthis have made significant territorial gains against Saudi-backed forces and have intensified attacks on strategic targets inside Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Arabia is in a “very difficult position” because it must protect military bases, government facilities and also oil infrastructure from Houthi drones and missiles, one regional official told AP.
A second official said Riyadh was seeking to rally international allies for a collective response to the Houthis, but added that “the decision now is to give diplomacy a chance.” Oman and Egypt are leading de-escalation efforts, according to AP.
Saudi Arabia has asked France, Britain, Pakistan, and Egypt to deploy air-defense support to help protect it from missiles and drones, the news agency reported.
US President Donald Trump said last week that his administration had declined a Saudi request to intervene militarily in Yemen in order to keep channels open with the Houthis. Axios reported that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called Trump twice to urge US strikes as Houthi forces advanced toward the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Last weekend, Oman hosted a meeting between US and Houthi representatives to discuss regional tensions, according to AP.
Watch RT’s report on the situation in Yemen, which has been suffering from a Saudi-imposed naval blockade for years.
The Houthis, who control much of western Yemen along the Red Sea coast, claimed this week that they had shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet. They released a video showing wreckage that appeared to belong to a Royal Saudi Air Force aircraft.
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia’s key East-West oil pipeline was also targeted by drones last week, forcing Riyadh to shut down the strategic route. Saudi authorities said the attack had originated in Iraq, while Iran-backed Iraqi militias denied responsibility. The pipeline allows Saudi crude exports to bypass the Strait of Hormuz and reach the Red Sea port of Yanbu.
The pipeline has become particularly important amid the US confrontation with Iran and disruption around the Strait of Hormuz. The US has seen its own stocks of missile interceptors decline during the conflict with Iran, limiting its ability to supply additional interceptors to Saudi Arabia.
As part of its response to the Sanaa strikes, the Houthis announced restrictions on Red Sea traffic involving Saudi oil. Their subsequent advances along Yemen’s western coast and seizure of strategic territory near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait have strengthened their ability to threaten shipping through the maritime chokepoint.

articles.title: US intervention in Yemen 'off the table' despite Saudi pressure
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US intervention in Yemen war 'off the table' despite Saudi pressure
Saudi Arabia has been pressing the United States to intervene against the Houthis after the Iran-backed group seized Yemen's Red Sea coast and the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, but Washington appears reluctant to enter the conflict.
American military intervention in Yemen is "completely off the table" before November's US midterm elections, a senior Yemeni researcher has told The New Arab, despite Riyadh's calls for military assistance to halt the Houthi advance.
Abdulghani al-Iryani, a senior researcher at the Sanaa Centre, told TNA that unless Iran and the Houthis dramatically escalate the situation, President Donald Trump is likely to stay out of the conflict in a bid to limit potential electoral damage for the Republican Party.
"I don't see a reason for the Republicans to give up their electoral chances for the sake of the Saudis," he said.
His comments come as American and Houthi officials held Oman-mediated talks over the weekend, during which US officials reportedly assured the group they would not intervene in the Yemen conflict.
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman reportedly urged President Trump to launch airstrikes against the Iran-backed group, which seized control of the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait on the Red Sea last week.
But sources say the Trump administration reached an understanding with the Houthis that Washington would stay out of the conflict even as the group attacks Saudi energy infrastructure and targets its ships in the Red Sea.
The Oman-mediated discussions saw the Houthis assure US officials that they would not target American ships and would uphold the 2025 ceasefire, according to Reuters.
A Yemeni source said Houthi officials also committed not to attack Israeli vessels or commercial ships that are not linked to Saudi Arabia.
The discussions, held at the US embassy in Muscat, involved senior Houthi officials Mohammad Abdulsalam and Abdelmalik al-Ajiri, sources said.
The Trump administration designated the Houthis as a foreign terrorist organisation in March 2025 before launching a two-month bombing campaign against them to halt their attacks on Red Sea shipping. That conflict ended after the two sides negotiated a ceasefire brokered by Oman.
The Houthis and the Yemeni government have engaged in fierce fighting since the collapse of the ceasefire in July.
The group has declared a blockade on Saudi ports and targeted Saudi ships in the Red Sea. It has also struck several Saudi energy sites, including oil refineries and pipelines.
The Houthis last week captured Yemen's entire Red Sea coastline, including the historic port of Mokha and Mayyun Island in the Bab al-Mandeb.
Since taking control of the area, the group has said it would uphold freedom of navigation through the strait but would continue to enforce its blockade on Saudi Arabia.
Few military options
Trump's refusal to intervene comes as the Houthis and their allies in Iraq attempt to shut down Saudi oil exports. Shipments via the Red Sea have been completely cut off after a drone strike last week took the East-West pipeline offline. The kingdom is now reliant exclusively on covert shipments via the Strait of Hormuz, assisted by the US military.
Saudi Arabia has escalated airstrikes against the Houthis in the week since they captured the Red Sea coast. The Houthis have reported more than 450 strikes as Riyadh tries to help government forces retake the area.
But analysts say Saudi Arabia's military options are limited. Airstrikes have done little to weaken the Houthis since Riyadh first launched its air campaign more than a decade ago, and it is hesitant to deploy ground troops inside the country.
Other allies have followed the US in declining to get involved in the conflict. Turkey and Pakistan have shown no willingness to intervene despite the three countries signing a mutual defence pact last month. Egypt's President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi is also unlikely to weigh in after discussing the situation with bin Salman in Cairo this week.
"I don't think Saudi military escalation will help the Yemeni cause or the Saudi cause," Al-Iryani told The New Arab.
"The best bet for Saudi Arabia is to try to help the government hold its ground until the US-Iran war is over, when it will be in a better position to negotiate with the Houthis," he said.

articles.title: Zelenskyy's Office explains how US Graham bill could affect Russia
articles.body:
Zelenskyy's Office explains how US Graham bill could affect Russia
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Ukraine's Presidential Commissioner for Sanctions Policy, has welcomed the US House of Representatives' passage of a bill co-authored by Senators Lindsey Graham and Richard Blumenthal that would enable the introduction of "punitive tariffs" on countries buying Russian energy, saying the measure would help reduce Russia's oil revenues.
Source: European Pravda, citing Vlasiuk in comments to journalists
Details: Vlasiuk welcomed the passage of the Graham-Blumenthal bill by the House of Representatives and said the legislation should become an important element of comprehensive pressure on Russia.
"Russia continues to receive significant revenues from oil sales, including through countries that continue to buy its energy resources... The tariffs envisaged by the bill against countries purchasing Russian energy could become an effective tool for reducing these revenues and increasing the cost of cooperation with Russia," the presidential commissioner said.
He also welcomed the fact that the sanctions cover Iran, noting that Moscow and Tehran have long cooperated in the defence industrial base, exchanged technologies and used shared supply channels, while Iranian drones and weapons components have become part of Russia's war against Ukraine.
"We expect the sanctions to make Russian energy exports more expensive, more difficult and less profitable. This does not mean an immediate end to the war, but it does mean gradually reducing Russia's ability to maintain the current intensity of its operations on the battlefield," Vlasiuk added.
Background:
- On 16 September, the US House of Representatives passed the Graham-Blumenthal bill that would enable the introduction of "punitive" tariffs on countries that buy Russian energy. The bill now awaits President Donald Trump's signature.
- The outcome marked a positive development after media reports suggested that the bill was encountering growing opposition in the US House of Representatives and could be blocked at least until the November congressional elections.
- The US Senate approved the bill on 7 August by 86 votes.

articles.title: Poland to Provide Ukraine With F-16 Ammunition
articles.body:
Poland is preparing a new military aid package for Ukraine that will include ammunition for F-16 fighter aircraft.
Polish Deputy Minister of National Defense Stanisław Wziątek said this, Polskie Radio reported.
Poland will also provide aviation equipment. The defense aid package could be worth €50 million.
The statement said that the ammunition for the aircraft included in the package would be used to destroy drones.
“Our assistance is being prepared. It will happen shortly. I cannot say what it contains, but I will say this: It is what Ukraine needs now. This includes, among other things, basic ammunition. This is ammunition mounted on F-16s to shoot down Russian drones,” Wziątek said.
Ukrainian F-16s use AIM-9 and AIM-120 air-to-air missiles against Russian aircraft. Last year, an F-16 armed with APKWS II rockets, which are effective against drones, was also spotted in Ukraine.
The aviation equipment Poland may provide could include drones or retired MiG-29 fighters. Warsaw is also considering providing Ukraine with Patriot missiles following the fall of a Kh-101 missile in Poland.

articles.title: ‘More Infantry, More Killed’: Russia’s Next Mobilization Could Backfire, Kyiv General Says
articles.body:
Russian forces have developed an infantry shortage over the past year, and another mobilization campaign would not necessarily solve the problem, a senior Ukrainian commander said Thursday.
Brig. Gen. Andriy Biletsky, commander of Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps, made the assessment during an interview with the national television marathon amid speculation that Moscow could announce another mobilization after Russia’s State Duma elections.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“They definitely have a better infantry [numbers] situation than we do. That is a fact,” Biletskyi said.
“But over the past year, we can conclude that the Russians have also developed an infantry shortage.”
Biletsky said he did not believe mobilization would radically change Russia’s battlefield position because deploying more soldiers would also lead to higher casualties.
“More infantry means more losses,” he said.
The general said the effectiveness of modern military operations increasingly depends on the organization of a reconnaissance-strike system capable of rapidly detecting and hitting targets. Drones and other sensors are central to that system, he added.
Rather than automatically producing battlefield gains, a larger Russian infantry force could provide Ukrainian units with more targets if their reconnaissance and strike capabilities remained effective, Biletsky said.
“More Russian infantry will mean more Russian soldiers killed,” he said, while acknowledging that a new mobilization would still create additional difficulties for Ukraine.
NBU Raises Key Rate to 16% as War-Driven Inflation Tops Forecast
Biletsky also argued that mobilized soldiers could have a greater effect on public opinion inside Russia than volunteer contract troops, particularly as casualties rise.
“The deaths among those mobilized will significantly contribute to social tension in Russia,” he said.
If Ukraine withstands the additional pressure, another Russian mobilization could ultimately accelerate internal problems within Russia.
“If we hold out, I think Russian mobilization could even be positive for us,” he said. “The processes of Russia’s internal disintegration will begin sooner.”
He added that some signs of those processes were already visible but had not yet reached a decisive level.
Former Russian President and current Russian Security Council Deputy Chair Dmitry Medvedev dismissed reports that Moscow is preparing a new wave of military mobilization, characterizing claims of an impending draft as false and provocative, Russian state news agency TASS reported on Friday, Sept. 11.
Medvedev claimed that reports suggesting Russia is on the verge of a mobilization call-up were fabricated to destabilize domestic public opinion ahead of elections to the State Duma, Russia’s lower house of parliament.
“To change that picture, they are spreading nonsense about Russia being ‘on the verge of mobilization,’” Medvedev said, arguing that such assertions were aimed at counterbalancing difficulties faced by the Armed Forces of Ukraine. “I deal with this matter directly on the instructions of the supreme commander-in-chief, so I can state with full responsibility: we have absolutely no need for mobilization.”

articles.title: Kyiv’s arms industry wants to kill the export fee. Parliament just refused to route that money to the army
articles.body:
Ukraine's arms industry wants the government to scrap a steep fee on weapons exports, warning it undercuts their prices just as Europe's defense market opens, RBC-Ukraine reported. The same fee has opened a second fight in Kyiv, where parliament this week declined to turn its revenue into money for the army.
Russia's war on Ukraine has pushed Europe into rearming, and Ukraine's battle-tested arms makers are among the few that can deliver at scale right now—an opening that domestic red tape could blunt, handing the advantage to competitors just as the market grows.
A €60 billion European window—and a fee in the way
The push comes as Europe opens a major market for Ukrainian weapons. The EU's €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan for 2026-2027 reserves €60 billion for defense purchases, and partners increasingly want weapons built on their own soil. International partners report more than 200 cooperation approaches to Ukrainian firms still without a decision, according to the industry's press release. Producers link the fee fix to Build with Ukraine, a co-production push they consider strategically significant.
Ukraine’s Build with Ukraine has 200-plus foreign cooperation bids pending decision. Its arms industry, representing 400-plus firms, wants to help fix mechanism
Parliament won't route the money to the army
On 15 September, the Verkhovna Rada—Ukraine's parliament—rejected a bill in first reading that would have sent fee revenue collected from 1 August 2026 into a special budget fund for the Defense Ministry, half for buying, modernizing, and repairing weapons, half for soldiers' pay. The vote left the fee itself untouched, since it rests on the Cabinet resolution, and settled only that its revenue will not be earmarked for the army.
The fee producers want gone
The Ukrainian Council of Arms Manufacturers, joined by other defense and employer groups, prepared proposals to rework the July government resolution, No. 875. They want the fee—20% on finished goods and technologies, 30% on parts—cut to zero, or capped at 5%. Firms must also pay upfront, before any foreign payment lands, with no refund guaranteed if a deal collapses. A UAH 15 million (about $337,000) threshold shuts out the small test shipments new clients often begin with.
Ukraine put an Italian-Swiss Skyguard into combat duty. The missile inside is a Cold War design derived from the American Sparrow
The fee has drawn complaints since the resolution took effect in early July. Ihor Fedirko, the council's executive director, earlier said the 30-day review window was welcome but warned it could clog into a bureaucratic queue as staff leave the agencies running it. One of the associations behind the submission calls the 30% rate on parts prohibitive, since Europe is where Ukrainian firms would undercut Chinese suppliers on price.
Ukraine has swung from banning weapons sales abroad to courting foreign buyers, and its defense sector now ranks among the country's fastest-growing industries. Wartime certification to NATO standards is turning that output into something European militaries can actually buy.

articles.title: How the Space Force Is Preparing for Its New Moving Target Missions
articles.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—As the Space Force prepares to field new fleets of satellites that can track moving targets in the air and on the ground, it’s working to ensure it has the organizational structures in place to onboard and operate those systems.
The U.S. military has long relied on large aircraft like the E-3 Sentry to track airborne targets, but leaders have become increasingly concerned that those platforms are vulnerable to long-range weapons. In recent years, the Space Force and the National Reconnaissance Office have been working to leverage satellites for the mission, an approach leaders expect will make the capability more resilient against adversaries’ anti-access/aerial-denial systems.
While the effort is still nascent and there’s much to prove about the ability of a satellite constellation to provide timely, clear tracks of moving targets like drones, missiles, and aircraft, the Pentagon has made some strides to demonstrate viability.
The NRO has launched some ground moving target indicator, or GMTI, satellites as part of its multimission proliferated low-Earth orbit constellation. And the head of Combat Forces Command, Lt. Gen. Gregory Gagnon, told reporters Sept. 16 that the Space Force expects to launch a new GMTI capability called Resilient Radar System-Ground in the next year or two. Those spacecraft are being built by Northrop Grumman, he said during a briefing at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference.
The Space Force is also on the verge of launching its first space-based air moving target indicator, or AMTI, satellites. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Sept. 14 the spacecraft would launch later this month. Acquisition officials have declined to detail how many satellites will launch or provide a date for the mission. The only Space Force launch scheduled for this month, according to Spaceflight Now’s public launch listing, is USSF-259, a classified payload slated to lift off Sept. 16 from Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif., on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.
The service awarded SpaceX a contract in May worth up to $4.2 billion to begin building out the AMTI constellation. The company is one of 12 vendors selected to compete for space-based AMTI contracts.
Col. Ryan Frazier, the Space Force’s portfolio acquisition executive for space-based sensing and targeting, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in July the service expects to have a “usable” space-based AMTI capability by 2028, noting that those satellites will be a first step toward an on-orbit targeting capability but not a full solution.
“Is it everything the joint force requires? I think that will probably extend beyond ‘28,” Frazier said. “But we are going to have capabilities they don’t have today. … We’ll be able to do things that are high-value or value-added. We won’t be able to do them everywhere all the time.”
Frazier told reporters Sept. 15 that the first space-based AMTI deliveries will provide a baseline for the rest of the architecture, allowing the Space Force to fine-tune and calibrate its satellites and processing algorithms.
“There’s a broader architecture that we need to build out for the joint force to be able to close on its long-range kill chain missions,” he said. “There’s how you battle manage with that data, how you apply the processing algorithms, get that data to the weapons and the shooters that you need, and the time latencies that requires.”
As the acquisition community develops and demonstrates new systems to perform the mission, the Space Force is standing up the operational units that will manage them. On July 31, CFC activated the 77th Surveillance Squadron within Space Delta 7. The role of the 77th is to take the intelligence collected by those AMTI and GMTI satellites and deliver it to decision-makers who will determine whether to attack a particular target.
“They will use information provided from the space layer, fuse that with other sources of information and intelligence, and make decisions about weapons engagement,” Gagnon said.
Meanwhile, U.S. Space Command is working with other combatant commands and the intelligence community to craft a concept of operations for the new mission area—a document that will describe how military operators will put the system to use. SPACECOM Commander Gen. Stephen Whiting told reporters Sept. 16 his team is working with the Space Force and the NRO to solidify a plan to transition those satellites to the command once they’re deemed ready for operations.
“This will be new and different as we elevate AMTI and GMTI to space,” Whiting said. “But we do have decades of lessons learned from AMTI and GMTI in other domains.”

articles.title: US lawmakers pass bill giving Trump more power to sanction Russia and its enablers
articles.body:
The US Congress has passed a sweeping bill allowing Donald Trump to raise tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy and issue other punishing sanctions against the Kremlin following a pitched battle between lawmakers backing Ukraine and sceptics worried the bill gives the president too much power.
The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 passed in a 262-159 vote on the last day before Congress goes on recess ahead of the midterm elections. Graham, who died earlier this year, co-authored and submitted the bill more than a year and a half ago.
The long delay in the vote was widely considered to be scepticism from the Trump administration, which had opposed additional sanctions and then recently changed its stance to support tabling the bill as efforts to negotiate with the Kremlin to end the war have yielded few results.
However the bill faced last-minute hurdles in Congress as members of the Republican party’s isolationist wing were joined by Democrats who warned that Trump could use the bill’s new tariffs authority against allies instead.
The bill would mandate new sanctions on Russian political and military officials, and foreign networks helping to supply Russia’s war machine and evade existing sanctions. It would also target Russia’s so-called fleet of “shadow tankers”, which have allowed the country to continue to ship crude around the world despite sanctions on its energy exports.
It would also allow Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top purchasers of Russian energy, including China, as well as other countries helping the Kremlin evade sanctions.
Senior Democrats voiced opposition to the bill during a heated floor debate. “Why in the world would this Congress give this president additional authority to visit that kind of economic harm on the American people?” said Hakeem Jeffries, the leading Democrat in the House, during a speech on Wednesday, adding he would vote against the bill.
Democratic staffers supporting the bill said that it offered a “last chance” to increase sanctions on Russia before Ukraine entered a “long winter”. Russia has improved the drone technology it has used to strike Ukrainian infrastructure as Kyiv has suffered a shortage of anti-air missiles, leaving the country in a dire position.
Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican supporting the bill, called it the US Congress’ “Churchill vs Chamberlain Moment on Russia”.
“Choking off the money funding a war of conquest in Europe is exactly what that authority should be used for, and Congress deciding to do that is Congress doing its constitutional job,” he said, rejecting arguments by Democrats that the bill gave Trump too much authority to slap tariffs on foreign countries.
The bill passed the Senate last month in a landslide 86-11 vote. However it faced more pushback in the House of Representatives. A Tuesday rule vote allowing consideration of Senate amendments to the bill passed by just 214-211, with two renegade Democrats joining Republicans to vote in favour of what they said was an act of support for Ukraine. That vote led to senior Democrats holding terse talks with their fellow party members.
“I’m proud to represent one of the largest Ukrainian communities in America – people who have lost fathers, mothers, sons and daughters in the fight to defeat fascism,” wrote Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, one of the two Democrat representatives, in a statement on Tuesday.
“I’ll always stand with my community’s values, and am grateful for the 86 senators who voted to send this bill to the House. My vote today gets us one step closer to enacting these sanctions into law and I look forward to voting tomorrow to cut off the flow of Russian oil money fuelling this war.”
The Ukrainian government has said it supported the bill, and hundreds of pro-Ukrainian activists calling for tougher sanctions on Russia held advocacy talks in Washington DC in the days leading up to the vote.
“We support any initiative that is in the interest of Ukraine and Ukrainians,” said Denys Sienik, the Chargé d’Affaires at the Ukrainian embassy in Washington DC. “So if we are talking about the possibility of putting more pressure on Russia so that it holds the Russian war machine, of course, we are there, and we are grateful to every senator, to every congressman and congresswoman for their voice and, and for their support.”

articles.title: “I can travel back to Finland and be safe. That is a luxury”: Sanna Marin on the Russian strike that stopped her train from Kyiv
articles.body:
Sanna Marin has made the journey to Kyiv and back many times since February 2022, in winter, summer, and autumn. Speaking at the Book 2.0 conference in Lisbon on Wednesday, days after returning from the September 2026 Yalta European Strategy conference, the former Finnish prime minister said this trip stood apart.
"This was the first time that I noticed so many drone alarms," she said. "I think there was only one missile alarm at that time we visited previously. Now in Kyiv, in this international meeting, I have never seen so many alarms going off when there's an international meeting, also with the US quite heavily represented there on site."
The knock at 5 a.m.
Marin was traveling back to Poland by train when the drone threat reached her carriage. "There was a knock on the door at 5 a.m. saying that we need to evacuate the train," she said. "I quickly put on my clothes and then saw what was happening. But then for some reason we were able to continue, so we never evacuated."
Another train on the same route was less fortunate. "Another train that was also traveling to Poland was evacuated several times, and it was also hit by a drone, and there was a missile that landed quite near as well."
That strike, on 13 September, hit the locomotive of a passenger train near the Polish border, at the Yahodyn crossing in Volyn Oblast. Ukraine's state railway operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, said the Russian drone may have been aimed at a diplomatic train carrying security advisers from several EU states and former European leaders, including former UK prime minister Boris Johnson, which had left the station earlier than scheduled as staff adjusted movements in real time. Former CIA director David Petraeus was on another train at the crossing during the attack.
Marin was careful not to assert what Russia intended. "I don't know what are the motives behind this. Was it just an accident where they're trying to hit a gas station, or whatever? So I don't know about the motives." A gas station near the Yahodyn crossing was indeed struck the same night, setting off a large fire.
A warning to Europe
What Marin could say was that the restraint she had seen on earlier visits was gone. "I think it is alarming that there isn't that kind of restraint any more from attacking when there are international people in Kyiv."
She read it as a message aimed at everyone who backs Ukraine, and framed her Lisbon remarks as a warning to Europe. "I think Putin is trying to send a signal that if you support Ukraine, we will bomb you. It's about creating fear. We shouldn't reply to that with fear but with determination."
Russia has made Ukraine's railways a deliberate target. It struck the network around 1,200 times in 2025, more than the previous two years combined, shifting its aim from track and stations to the rolling stock itself, and about 40 railway workers have been killed since 2022, according to Ukrzaliznytsia. Strikes on trains have averaged about six a day since early March.
Why the west is suddenly in range
Trending Now
Western regions were long considered safer because of their distance from the front. Two changes have brought them within reach, and what Marin noticed on this trip is the product of both.
The first is control range. Russia's drones are steered in real time only within a "red zone" near the border and the front, and until recently that zone did not reach the west. Russia extended it by building signal repeaters on towers and rooftops in Belarus, boosting Shahed control signals far enough to reach Kyiv, Rivne, and Volyn.
Ukrainian hackers exposed the network in February 2026, and by June President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was giving Belarus's Aliaksandr Lukashenka one week to strip the repeaters from its border towers, warning that if Belarus did not, Ukraine would. Russia has also used signal-relay balloons drifting from Belarus to keep its drones connected.
The second is speed. Ukrainian interceptor drones had learned to bring down about half of the incoming Shaheds by mid-2026, up from roughly 10% over the winter, so Russia reached for jet power: the jet-powered Geran-4 is built to fly at up to 500 kilometers an hour, several times faster than the piston-engine drones Ukraine spent three years learning to intercept.
Jet-powered Gerans now make up a large and growing share of Russia's nightly launches, and the largest model, the Geran-5, is credited with a range of up to 1,000 kilometers, far enough to put Warsaw within reach of the drone bases Russia has built near its borders. The near-miss on a diplomatic train two kilometers from Poland is what that reach looks like at its western edge.
"That is a luxury"
Marin said she had not felt afraid on the train, and drew the distinction herself.
"Ukrainian people are living in fear every single day. I can travel back to Finland and be safe with my family. I think that is a luxury."
She said she would return. "I didn't feel intimidated or afraid, and I will definitely go back."

articles.title: Greenpeace exposes Russian disinformation over strikes on Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant
articles.body:
Greenpeace exposes Russian disinformation over strikes on Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant
Russia is deliberately sabotaging power supply lines at the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP). More than half of all cases of total loss of off-site power at the plant since 2022 have occurred over the last seven months.
Source: Greenpeace Ukraine
Details: A new analysis by Greenpeace Ukraine found no evidence of the claimed Ukrainian strikes.
Quote: "Russia is intentionally carrying out sabotage and deliberately disabling ZNPP power supply lines."
Details: The new investigation by Greenpeace Ukraine, conducted jointly with London-based McKenzie Intelligence Services (MIS), exposes a Russian disinformation campaign claiming that Ukrainian artillery strikes and drone attacks caused severe damage to critical infrastructure providing power to the ZNPP.
Analysis of high-resolution satellite imagery conducted by MIS found no evidence to support Russian claims of a Ukrainian artillery strike on 10 February 2026 or a UAV attack on 4 June 2026 targeting the Ferrosplavna 330 kV switchyard near the Zaporizhzhia Thermal Power Plant.
The analysis found no evidence of the claimed attack by over 20 Ukrainian UAVs on 4 June 2026 as asserted by Russia. The damage attributed by Russia to an alleged drone attack on 4 June was already present before that date.
Damage to the switchyard unit has been confirmed; however, satellite data does not support Russian assertions that it was caused by Ukrainian artillery strikes or drone attacks.
The Ferrosplavna 330 kV line is one of two off-site power transmission lines providing electricity to the ZNPP.
The other line – the Dniprovska 750 kV line – has been out of service since 22 May 2026, when Russian military attacks caused severe damage to the Dniprovska substation, located approximately 100 km north of the ZNPP.
Russia is intensifying attacks on the Ukrainian power grid, and their impact on nuclear safety is becoming increasingly severe.
Quote from Shaun Burnie, nuclear specialist at Greenpeace Ukraine: "Repeated cases of off-site power loss at the ZNPP are the result of Russian military attacks on Ukraine's energy grid and sabotage at the ZNPP and its associated open switchyards."
Details: Off-site power supply is critical for nuclear safety as it is required to run key reactor safety systems, including pumps that ensure the cooling of nuclear fuel in reactor cores and spent fuel pools.
The ZNPP has six reactor units and six spent fuel pools containing hundreds of tonnes of highly radioactive nuclear fuel. Since Russian troops seized the plant in 2022, the ZNPP has experienced 26 complete losses of off-site power. Fourteen of these cases have occurred since February 2026.
Every complete loss of off-site power forces the ZNPP to rely on emergency diesel generators to maintain critical nuclear safety functions.
Background:
- Earlier, Energoatom emphasised that the actual condition of the temporarily occupied ZNPP points to a continued erosion of fundamental nuclear safety principles.
- Energoatom previously warned that every blackout at the occupied ZNPP degrades the condition of its equipment, particularly the diesel generator units supplying backup power to the station.
